headline: Punjab BJP forms state election committee for 2027 Assembly polls
content: <p>Chandigarh: Punjab BJP chief Kewal Singh Dhillon on Monday announced the formation of a state election committee to accelerate preparations for the 2027 assembly elections in the state.</p>.<p>Besides Dhillon, the committee comprised national vice president Manpreet Singh Badal, Rajya Sabha MP Tarun Chugh, former state unit presidents Ashwani Sharma, Sunil Jakhar, Avinash Rai Khanna, Manoranjan Kalia, Shwait Malik, Vijay Sampla, state general secretary (organization) Manthri Srinivasulu and former union ministers Preneet Kaur, Ravneet Singh Bittu.</p>.<p>State secretary Manjit Singh Manna, former minister Rana Gurmit Singh Sodhi, MLA Jangi Lal Mahajan and former MLA Dinesh Babbu were also part of the committee.</p>.Have a say in 2027 Punjab Assembly polls? BJP launches phone lines, QR code to seek ideas.<p>Apart from this, MP and party's Punjab in-charge Satish Poonia, state co-incharges Virendra Sachdeva and Alka Gurjar have been included as special invitees in the state election committee.</p>.<p>Dhillon said that the state election committee would play an important role in further strengthening the party's strategy, election preparations and organisational activities for the upcoming assembly elections.</p>.<p>He said the BJP is fully committed to living up to the expectations of the people of Punjab and taking the state forward on the path of development, prosperity and stability.</p>

headline: Delhi Public School, Karnal, organises Scholar Badge Ceremony
content: Delhi Public School, Karnal, organised its Scholar Badge Ceremony 2025-26, celebrating the academic accomplishments, dedication, perseverance and exemplary achievements of its students. The ceremony was graced by Manan Sham Gupta, management member, as the guest of honour. The ceremony was held under the guidance of Principal Savita Saluja. Scholar badges were conferred upon deserving students in recognition of their scholastic excellence, while special recognition was also accorded to students achieving 100 per cent attendance, who were presented with special trophies. The ceremony included the presentation of gold medals, blue tie, blue blazer, and blue and green scholar badges, acknowledging the diverse milestones achieved by students across the CBSE and Cambridge curricula.

headline: Delhi Govt planning to sell prime Jal Board properties: AAP
content: The AAP on Sunday accused the BJP-led Delhi government of planning to sell prime Delhi Jal Board (DJB) properties in areas such as Greater Kailash, Lajpat Nagar and Jhandewalan, questioning its claim of making the utility profitable through better governance.Addressing the issue, AAP Delhi president Saurabh Bharadwaj alleged that the government’s promise of improving the DJB’s financial position through better administration appeared to have fallen flat, with the focus now shifting to generating revenue from its land and buildings.Sharing an alleged DJB board resolution on X, Bharadwaj said the proposal envisaged appointing a transaction advisor to assess, redevelop, monetise and commercially utilise the board’s land and building assets across Delhi to enhance revenue.He questioned whether the government intended to sell the water utility’s valuable properties instead of improving its functioning and financial management.Bharadwaj also claimed that the DJB’s billing scheme had failed despite repeated extensions of its deadlines.

headline: Delhi saw 1,210 deaths in building collapse, fire, civic mishaps this year
content: As many as 1,210 people have lost their lives in Delhi so far this year in different incidents of building collapses, fires and other incidents exposing deficient infrastructure and chinks in the safety regulatory oversight in the national capital.Data from Delhi Fire Services (DFS) revealed that while 91 people lost their lives in fire incidents, the remaining 1,119 died in various building collapses and other crumbling civic infrastructure incidents, translating into four deaths everyday.The deaths reveal disturbing evidence of severely deficient civic infrastructure and regulatory oversight in Delhi that have led to such incidents.October month recorded the highest deaths this year as 144 people lost their lives, including 8 due to fires, according to the data.The highest fire related deaths were recorded in June when 25 people lost their lives.The fire department data shows the city recorded a total of 17,074 calls of fire incidents, while a total of 4,074 emergency calls were made for other civic apathies including building collapses, the data showed.The numbers of deaths due to fire remain highest in the last three years as in 10 months only 91 deaths have been reported in comparison to 84 deaths in the 2025–26 financial year and 90 deaths in 2024–25.As per an earlier data shared by the DFS, the city recorded 396 house-collapse calls through October 26, 2026, with 321 calls logged between April and October (down 27% from 441 during the same seven-month window in 2025).This includes, one of the deadliest incident occurred on September 6, 2026, when a five-storey residential building operating as a boys' PG hostel ("Hostel Daze") in Satya Niketan collapsed, killing at least seven people and injuring several others amid heavy rains and basement renovation work.A month later on October 7, 2026, a multi-storey residential building collapsed in Northeast Delhi's New Seemapuri area, claiming three lives (including a child) and injuring others.Another fatal incident struck Harsh Vihar on October 25, 2026, killing a father and son at an old structure with a lower-ground godown reportedly during lintel work. Most recently, on November 5, 2026, a three-storey building under construction collapsed in Old Delhi's Chawri Bazaar (Gali Sattara), killing two construction workers and prompting municipal suspensions and safety inquiries.The 91 deaths in fire includes, deadliest major fire in Delhi in 2026 occurred on June 3, 2026, at the Flourish Stay bed-and-breakfast hotel in South Delhi’s Malviya Nagar neighborhood. The blaze originated in the basement pantry and ground-floor restaurant before rapidly spreading through the five-story building, killing 21 to 22 people—including several foreign nationals visiting Delhi for medical treatment—and injuring over 40 others.Subsequent investigations revealed severe safety violations, as the establishment was operating 25 rooms without a Fire Department 'No Objection Certificate' and had only a single entry and exit point.In addition to this tragedy, Delhi experienced several other significant industrial and commercial fires through the year, including a fatal blaze at a Mangolpuri shoe factory in late October that killed four workers, a large garment factory fire in Najafgarh in early November, and back-to-back incidents in mid-November involving a scrap warehouse fire in Mundka and a deadly basement fire during welding work in Lajpat Nagar.

headline: Delhi, NCR states miss most air pollution targets: Government review
content: A Central government-monitored review of this year’s air pollution control action plans of Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh has assessed the progress made by the four states across 29 indicators, including waste management, industrial pollution, road dust and vehicular emissions. Most targets, according to the assessment, have not been met. The report has evaluated achievements against annual targets, as of October 31. It has rated 100% target achievement as ‘Satisfactory’, over 75% achievement as ‘Needs Improvement’, and those below 75% as ‘Unsatisfactory’. Delhi is leading in monitoring and industry sectors. The city has installed all 19 targeted air-quality monitoring stations and conducted 1,609 industrial inspections against a target of 979. All 90 targeted industries have installed both online emission monitoring systems and air pollution control devices. At 1,296 against 539, the Capital has met its target set for diesel generator set inspections. The target set for construction and demolition waste processing capacity has also been achieved, at 1,000 tonnes per day. Delhi, however, has added no municipal solid waste processing capacity against its target of 650 tonnes per day, and neither of its two targeted plants has been made operational. For legacy waste at its three landfill sites, Okhla has processed 18.26 lakh metric tonnes against a target of 27.45 lakh, Bhalswa 27.49 lakh against 48.42 lakh, and Ghazipur 16.53 lakh against 39.12 lakh. Construction and demolition waste offtake stands at 21% of target for government agencies and 26% for private agencies. None of Delhi’s 49 targeted green crematoria has been established either. The report on enforcement and transport related progress is mixed. While the city has added 1,703 city buses against a target of 2,395, and 19 against 35 large road-sweeping machines, it has deployed only such medium machine against a target of 57. It has met its short-term decongestion target (34 of 34), but completed only eight of 28 long-term points. For parking infrastructure, the number stands at 15 against 266 lots. The report has also recorded 7.09 lakh pollution-under-control certificate violations against a target of 11.72 lakh, a figure it rates as ‘Unsatisfactory’. Delhi crossed its targets for EV charging stations (6,000 against 5,000) and last-mile connectivity vehicles (810 against 800). Widest gaps in Haryana Haryana, the report shows, has the widest gaps. It has not installed any air quality stations against a target of 23 and has conducted only 177 industrial inspections against a goal of 3,865. It also recorded no government offtake of construction and demolition waste. The state also lags behind in terms of measures to tackle vehicular pollution. Against a target of 11,607, only 2,584 (22%) industrial inspections were conducted. No Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) systems have been deployed at petrol pumps in Haryana, Rajasthan or UP, against their combined target of 4,129. Delhi and the other three states have added a total of 1,893 city buses — including Delhi’s 1,703 — against a combined goal of 3,645. Like Delhi, the other states too have not set up any green crematorium. The four states have crossed the target set for functional crop residue management machines — at 35,077 against 32,906. For ex-situ straw utilisation, however, the number stands at 72.10 lakh tonnes against a goal of 1.05 crore tonnes, and pellet and briquette utilisation at 18.99 lakh tonnes against 42.06 lakh tonnes.

headline: Delhi Nursery Admissions 2027-28 schedule out, schools upload intake-criteria at edudel.nic.in
content: Private schools in Delhi will start uploading their admission criteria and the points assigned to each criterion for entry-level classes today, November 23, on the official website, edudel.nic.in. The Directorate of Education (DoE) Delhi, earlier announced the admission schedule for entry-level classes in private unaided recognised schools. The application process will begin on December 1, and parents will have until December 28 to register and submit forms. This year’s admission cycle will also see the introduction of two additional pre-primary entry classes, lower kindergarten (LKG) and upper kindergarten (UKG), as Delhi moves towards a three-year foundational stage in line with the NEP 2020. The revised structure will operate alongside Nursery admissions, with different age requirements and admission provisions for each class. Delhi Nursery Admissions 2027-28: Important dates Admission event Date Uploading of admission criteria and points begins November 23, 2026 Admission process and availability of forms begins December 1, 2026 Last date to submit application forms December 28, 2026 Schools upload applicant details and points awarded January 4, 2027 Parents can raise queries or objections regarding points January 5 to 11, 2027 Display of final points after resolving objections January 12, 2027 First list of selected children, including waiting list January 20, 2027 Queries regarding the first selection list January 21 to 28, 2027 Second selection list, if applicable February 5, 2027 Queries regarding the second selection list February 6 to 12, 2027 Subsequent admission list, if required February 22, 2027 Closure of admission process March 12, 2027 Note that the above schedule applies only to open seats in private unaided recognised schools; admissions for EWS, DG, and CWSN others will be held separately. Delhi Nursery Admissions 2027-28: Age criteria explained One of the key aspects of this year's admission process is the phased implementation of the revised foundational-stage structure. The age requirements will be calculated as on March 31, 2027. Under the revised structure, the three pre-primary stages will be Nursery (Balvatika 1), Lower KG (Balvatika 2) and Upper KG (Balvatika 3), followed by Class 1. The age requirements for the 2027-28 session are: Class Minimum and maximum age as on March 31, 2027 Nursery (Balvatika 1 / Pre-School 1) 3+ years and up to 4 years (New Admissions) Lower KG (Balvatika 2 / Pre-School 2) 4+ years and up to 5 years Upper KG (Balvatika 3 / Pre-School 3) 5+ years and up to 6 years Class 1 5+ years and up to 6 years for students moving from KG under the existing structure For Nursery admission, a child must have completed three years of age by March 31, 2027. The age criteria will also apply to fresh admissions in the newly introduced Lower KG and Upper KG classes, where applicable. The Directorate has clarified that children enrolled in Nursery during the 2026-27 academic session will move to Lower KG in 2027-28. At the same time, schools can admit new students directly to Lower KG, provided they have completed four years of age by March 31, 2027. Similarly, Upper KG will be introduced as a new entry-level class in the 2027-28 session. Fresh admissions will be allowed for children who have completed five years of age by March 31, 2027. Students who were enrolled in KG during the last cycle will move to Class 1 in 2027-28 under the earlier structure. The transition is therefore being implemented in phases rather than requiring all existing students to move through the new three-year pre-primary structure at once. Delhi Nursery Admissions 2027-28: Where and how to check admission criteria? Parents will be able to check the criteria under the 'admission criteria (2027-28)' section in the 'What's New' section of the official DoE website. If schools don't upload their admission rules on time, their admissions might be put on hold, the DoE said in its notice. The Directorate has also reiterated that schools cannot use criteria previously prohibited by it and upheld by the Delhi High Court. These include parameters such as parents' educational qualifications, whether both parents are working, the child's first-born status, proficiency in music or sports, and other arbitrary or discriminatory considerations. Schools must also publish the criterion-wise break-up of points awarded to applicants. After applications close, schools will publish the names of applicants and the points awarded to each child on January 4. Parents will have seven days, from January 5 to 11, to raise queries or objections if they believe the points have been incorrectly assigned. Schools will have to respond to these queries and publish the final points on January 12. If two or more applicants secure identical points for the last available seats, schools will have to conduct a draw of lots. The process must be transparent and held in the presence of parents and the designated Education Department nominee. Schools must inform eligible parents at least five days before the draw, conduct the process under videography and retain the recording. Delhi Nursery Admissions 2027-28: Important documents required For admission-related verification, the Directorate has listed the following documents as valid proof of residence of the child or parents: -Ration card or smart card issued in the name of either parent, carrying the child's name. -Domicile certificate of the child or either parent. -Voter identity card (EPIC) of either parent. -Electricity, MTNL telephone or water bill in the name of either parent or the child. -Passport in the name of either parent or the child. -Aadhaar card or UID card issued in the name of either parent. Parents should check the individual school's admission instructions for any additional documents required during verification. The overall admission process for the 2027-28 academic session will conclude on March 12, 2027. The Directorate has also directed schools to publish the details of selected candidates and waiting lists, along with the points awarded, to ensure transparency in the admission process.

headline: Ehsaas moves needle on students’ mental health
content: For far too long, the emotional and psychological well-being of students has remained peripheral to India’s education system, preoccupied as it is with examinations, competition, outcomes. Ehsaas 2026, Delhi’s mental health and well-being policy for schools and higher educational institutions, is a welcome and long-overdue recognition that education must concern itself with more than academic performance. According to the National Crime Records Bureau’s Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India 2024 report, released in May this year, 14,488 students died by suicide in India in 2024, a 4.3 per cent increase over 13,892 in 2023. Between 2015 and 2024, student suicides have risen by more than 62 per cent and account for approximately 8.5 per cent of all recorded suicides in India. These figures, which include students across school and higher education, are deeply concerning. Academic pressure, family circumstances, social isolation, bullying, and uncertainty about the future can intersect in ways that are difficult for young people to articulate. Against this backdrop, Ehsaas marks an important shift — it moves the needle on mental health being treated as an institutional responsibility, not just an individual or family concern. The policy’s provisions for school counsellors, helplines, district-level well-being centres, teacher and parent training, and a structured escalation mechanism are significant steps towards making schools safer, more responsive spaces. Yet, the policy should be viewed as only a first step in a longer journey. The proposed ratio of one counsellor for every 500 school students is a useful starting point, but it may prove inadequate in practice, given the different circumstances and needs of each student. Counsellors must be adequately trained and appointed on a regular basis, rather than being treated as a compliance measure. District-level facilities must have the personnel and resources to ensure that referrals translate into timely interventions. The National Education Policy 2020 envisaged a broader understanding of education, moving away from rote learning towards creativity and the nurturing of individual potential. It recognised that inclusive classrooms, manageable workloads, access to extracurricular opportunities, career guidance and avenues to future employment play a big part in student well-being. Ehsaas deserves credit for placing mental health within that conversation. Its success will depend on whether it brings about a meaningful change in the everyday experience of students: Whether they feel heard and seen, and whether they can look beyond the classroom with a sense of confidence, dignity and possibility.

headline: Sachchida Nand Tripathi at Idea Exchange: ‘For significant AQI change, we must cross threshold to transition to clean energy and transportation’
content: IIT Kanpur professor Sachchida Nand Tripathi on the gaps in India’s air pollution response, the need to link health impacts to different pollution levels and why we can’t see clouds in Delhi. He was in conversation with Amitabh Sinha, Deputy Editor, and Nikhil Ghanekar, Assistant Editor, of The Indian Express Amitabh Sinha: It has been more than a decade since we have been taking concrete measures to fight air pollution. But despite the monitoring issue being addressed adequately, there hasn’t been even marginal improvement in air quality. If anything, the situation gets worse every year. Where is the gap? Monitoring has helped address several issues. In the three major states known to have farm fires — Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh — there has been a marginal decrease in fire counts compared to 2025. We have possibly not seen the improvements we would like because there is a threshold that needs to be crossed in transitioning to cleaner sources of energy and transportation. A large fraction of the population still uses solid fuel for cooking. Delhi’s particulate loading is also contributed by traffic exhaust. To see significant difference, we need major changes in these two sectors and bring farm fires down to a much lower level. Nikhil Ghanekar: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) recently clarified why readings went blank on Diwali night when pollution levels crossed a certain threshold. Should we continue with this kind of cap? How can it affect our response, given that short periods of high exposure can affect vulnerable populations? Every machine is calibrated for a particular range. Beyond that, its accuracy starts going down. So, I would not worry much if readings cross the range for which the machine is calibrated. There are other ways of monitoring pollution in Delhi, including sensors and satellites, which provide reasonably accurate information. If the government monitoring network is unable to provide information momentarily, multimodal data from other sources should still give us the complete picture. On linking health with AQI levels | Even at 200 and 300, clear health outcomes have to be specified so that citizens know what is happening to them. This could give policymakers a better understanding to speed up measures Nikhil Ghanekar: Do we need to move beyond generalising AQI above 500 as hazardous for all and specify how severe the health impact can be at different levels? Health outcomes have to be precisely linked to different AQI levels. Even at 200 and 300, clear health outcomes have to be specified so that citizens know what is happening to their health. This could also give policymakers a much better understanding and help speed up measures. Sarwat Fatima: How do you control pollution practically when every solution — be it for firecrackers, cars, factories and construction — is met with an argument? A study we conducted across the NCR and the Gangetic plain states between October 8 and February 8, looked at the primary emission sources: informal-sector burning, stubble burning and industries. If these three sources are reduced by 80 per cent, Delhi’s AQI, which was around 290 last year, could come down to 120-130. There are win-win solutions. If every household has access to LPG and electricity for space and water heating, burning can be eliminated. If waste burning on roads is completely stopped, AQI can reach 120-130. Similarly, if we increase the number of buses, all electric, AQI could come down to 70-80 or even 60. Nikhil Ghanekar: If you were an administrator rather than a scientist, what are the issues you would immediately address to reduce pollution? And what is the silver lining in the measures taken so far? The Delhi-NCR region now has a fairly dense monitoring network. We are also working with agencies to create a hybrid monitoring network, undertake hyperlocal monitoring and identify gaps where interventions can be designed in time. Many emissions blind spots need attention — waste that is not properly managed and gets burned, or construction sites that are not adequately protected. These are places where real-time interventions can help avoid or reduce pollution spikes. On cloud seeding | Studies have highlighted a limitation during winter: the lack of clouds. In their absence, you cannot seed anything. Optimising it would require much more effort before we can succeed The second issue requires high-level policy intervention. The LPG network expanded over the last seven to eight years, but for various reasons people have dropped out. We need to address this. The Commission for Air Quality Management covers Delhi-NCR districts and Rajasthan. We can design an instrument to connect every household to LPG. We also need to address public transport. While we have the metro, for last-mile connectivity, people still rely on other polluting modes. We should ensure that vehicles ferrying people for public and private sector units and schools are EVs. This year, Delhi’s atmospheric ventilation coefficient was 8 per cent weaker than last year. The atmosphere’s ability to push out pollutants has weakened. If we make changes of only 7-8 per cent, they will be offset. We have to plan for weather conditions that are beyond our control. Anuradha Mascarenhas: Do air quality issues in cities like Pune, Mumbai and Nashik affect rainfall patterns? There is a whole body of research globally and in India on a phenomenon called the aerosols’ indirect effect. Aerosols can suppress or, depending on the threshold, increase rainfall. This is called the cloud microphysical effect. Aerosols act as nuclei to form cloud droplets. A large amount of aerosols competes for the same amount of water vapour, modifying cloud microphysics and consequently altering rainfall frequency and rates. This is a well-studied phenomenon, including its consequences for the Indian monsoon. Nikhil Ghanekar: Why doesn’t the AQI worsen as much in Punjab as it does in Delhi when paddy straw is burnt? We don’t know, partly because Punjab does not have as dense a monitoring network as Delhi. Fire counts started increasing around October 27-28, peaked around November 4-5, subsided a little and have started increasing again. This is exactly the period when winds blow from the Northwest. The source is in Punjab but the emissions are carried towards Delhi. Delhi also has a much larger vehicle fleet and more industries surrounding it. The five or six districts in Punjab prone to stubble burning do not have the same population density as Delhi-NCR. These compounded factors make Delhi far more polluted. Western UP also has some burning but pollution does not reach Delhi’s levels. Delhi has peculiar meteorological conditions and is a tabletop city at an altitude of 220 metres. These factors make its air more polluted than that of surrounding regions. Abhimanyu Hazarika: What is the efficacy of anti-smog guns used by the government? Have there been impact studies? What kind of water is used, and can it lead to secondary particles? I understand that IIT Delhi has assessed the efficacy of anti-smog guns. If I recall correctly, they are effective only over a small volume around where they are operating. As for the water used, I am not aware whether it is fresh or treated water. Alok Singh: Cloud seeding is back in the news, with government authorities trying to determine whether they can induce rain. Should we continue with this experiment? Several studies have highlighted a serious limitation during winter: the lack of clouds. In their absence, you cannot seed anything. Cloud seeding is both art and science. You need a reasonable amount of experimentation because several parameters can affect the outcome. Optimising it would require much more effort before we can succeed in getting winter rains through it. Nirbhay Thakur: Do we need awareness campaigns to encourage public transport? The AI centre at IIT Kanpur is working with the Delhi Transport Corporation on route optimisation. The existing buses in Delhi are not catering to everyone who needs them. When more buses come, we have to redesign the routes. A massive public awareness campaign is also needed. It has to be a twin approach: Make people aware while also discouraging private transport. Once adequate public transport is available, policy interventions should ensure that those who continue to bring their own vehicles, pay more. Shiny Varghese: EVs have heavy batteries, which means that when their tyres hit the road, PM2.5 particles could increase. Are EVs really a solution then? We conducted a study in Delhi in 2018-19 to estimate the contribution of brake and tyre wear to PM2.5 and found that it was non-negligible but also not very high — around 5-6 per cent. For heavy EVs, I would imagine that they might have different kinds of tyres that can sustain friction without significantly increasing particulate matter from road wear. But we need data. But prima facie, I would say it is prudent to go for EVs because cutting tailpipe emissions will outweigh emissions from tyre wear. Sophiya Mathew: IITM has added real-time source apportionment data that accounts for firecracker emissions. But there is a huge standard deviation. How accurate is this data, given that aerosols are chemically complex and mix with other emissions? We have measured the contribution of firecrackers to particulate matter by looking at elemental composition. You use a range of mass spectrometers, including a metal monitor, which can measure a set of elements. Some of these clearly point to emissions originating from firecrackers. These elements do not easily combine with other organics and, even if they do, they can still be measured in their elemental form. Sophiya Mathew: How are anthropogenic sources like road dust and construction dust differentiated in source apportionment studies, given that their chemical nature can be similar? One thing that differentiates anthropogenic combustion sources from mechanical sources is particle size. Industry and combustion emissions generally come in PM2.5, while road and construction dust generally comes in PM10. We also look at elemental composition and compare the ratios with those found in pristine dust or earth’s crustal material. This helps identify whether emissions are coming from dust or firecrackers. Nikhil Ghanekar: What is the life cycle of the dust particle coming from different sources, including the Thar desert and man-made dust? If green cover decreases, it leads to greater erosion and dust can be lifted by wind more easily. Once airborne, it can be transported. We need to plant more trees and arrest desertification. Dust particles are generally larger in size, often above 2.5 micrometres, and heavier than other particles like soot and therefore settle faster. However, if strong vertical winds lift them, particularly before the monsoon during convection, they can form elevated layers of dust. If coated, they can act as cloud condensation nuclei or ice nuclei. Even without coating, dust is a good ice nucleus. It can become a seed for ice-particle formation in clouds, at altitudes of six or seven kilometres. At that point, the time it stays in the atmosphere increases. Close to the surface, however, dust generally settles much sooner than anthropogenic particles such as soot, organics, sulphate and nitrate, which tend to remain in the atmosphere longer. Nikhil Ghanekar: There has been considerable debate over retrofitting thermal power plants with devices to reduce sulphur emissions. Three institutions — IIT Delhi, National Institute of Advanced Studies (NIAS) and National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI) — reportedly recommended that these devices were not necessary because ground-level SO2 concentrations were not high. Instead, they recommended electrostatic precipitators to cut particulate emissions. Have we established that power plants do not lead to significant transboundary secondary pollutants? Power plants emit ash particles and soot, which are primary particles. Electrostatic precipitators can be installed to address these. Then, there are gases such as sulphur dioxide, which can transform into sulphate and become secondary pollutants. Some sulphur dioxide quickly transitions into sulphate because particles in India are slightly alkaline in nature. Sulphur dioxide is acidic and can quickly react to form sulphate in those particles. That may explain why we see low sulphur dioxide in the atmosphere. One could look at plants with Flue-gas Desulfurisation (FGD) installed and study their effect on sulphur dioxide emissions and the formation of secondary pollutants nearby. Nikhil Ghanekar: What are the short- and medium-term prescriptions you would offer before we sign off? Effective waste disposal would dramatically reduce waste combustion and burning on roads. This requires a waste management strategy and greater capacity in municipal corporations across the Indo-Gangetic plain. We also need to almost eradicate farm fires through incentives and crop diversification. We are working with several municipal corporations and the Delhi government to bring intelligence into the system and create standard operating procedures that officials can implement in real time. The system can help them assess what works and what doesn’t. It is time to start implementing these SOPs using the information and decision-making support available. Delhi also has a much larger vehicle fleet and more industries surrounding it. The five or six districts in Punjab prone to stubble burning do not have the same population density as Delhi-NCR. These compounded factors make Delhi far more polluted. Western UP also has some burning, but pollution does not reach Delhi’s levels. Delhi has peculiar meteorological conditions and is a tabletop city at an altitude of 220 metres. These factors make its air more polluted than that of surrounding regions. One could look at plants with Flue-gas Desulfurisation (FGD) installed and study their effect on sulphur dioxide emissions and the formation of secondary pollutants nearby.

headline: 'Couldn't even fill single Ramlila Maidan': BJP's Nitin Nabin takes jibe at Rahul's 'vote chori' rally
content: NEW DELHI: BJP national president Nitin Nabin on Monday targeted Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over his 'vote chori' allegations, claiming the INDIA bloc had failed to fill even a single Ramlila Maidan during its rally in Delhi. Addressing a BJP rally in Karimnagar, Telangana, Nabin said BJP workers had drawn larger crowds across more than 200 locations and accused Rahul of advocating for alleged infiltrators to be included in voter lists."Rahul Gandhi ji used to say that vote chori took place. Rahul ji, the people are with us, and the votes are with us. The people of Karimnagar have shown that their blessings are with us. They (the INDIA alliance), despite putting in their all, couldn't even fill a single Ramlila Maidan, while BJP workers gathered far more people than could fit in a Ramlila Maidan at over 200 locations," news agency ANI quoted him as saying.Nabin also questioned Rahul Gandhi's claim that 13 crore votes had been stolen and challenged his stand on the inclusion of people whose whereabouts were allegedly unverified."Rahul ji claimed that 13 crore people's votes had been stolen. But I would like to ask: Why should 3 crore people be included in the voter list? More than 6 crore people have shifted. I know that in Telangana, lakhs of people have shifted their votes. So, should people be allowed to vote twice? The remaining 3 crore are those whose whereabouts the Election Commission enquired about in 2003, but they have no answers. So, the person advocating for these 3 crore infiltrators is none other than Rahul Gandhi," he said.Nabin targets INDIA bloc over vote theft allegationsThe BJP chief accused opposition parties of attempting to create chaos, while asserting that the BJP was receiving public support through democratic means."They tried to spread chaos—let them have their chaos! We, on the other hand, are receiving democracy's blessings," Nabin said.Taking a swipe at Rahul Gandhi's references to the Constitution, he said, "I have come to tell those who carry a copy of the Constitution around in their hands: you have a copy of the Constitution in your hands, but the Constitution is in our hearts. You speak of the Constitution, but we revere it. That is why we respect all constitutional institutions."He also invoked the Emergency to target the Congress, saying, "The people who murdered democracy by imposing the Emergency to save their own seats are today invoking democracy."Nabin also criticised Rahul Gandhi's remarks on India's economy, accusing him of insulting the country both within India and abroad."Whenever Rahul Gandhi is in the country, he does nothing but insult it, and he insults it abroad too. Rahul ji goes everywhere saying that India's economy is a disaster. Rahul ji, India's economy and its development are advancing on a global scale. Today, India has moved beyond the Fragile Five to become the world's fourth-largest economy," he said.Expressing confidence about the BJP's prospects in Telangana, Nabin said the party would hold the state government accountable."I am sure the countdown to the Telangana government has begun. BJP karyakartas will now hold the Telangana government accountable," he said.He also predicted that Prime Minister Narendra Modi would return to the Red Fort in 2029."Modi ji will not go anywhere; he will appear on the ramparts of the Red Fort again in 2029. Rahul ji, keep dreaming. India's youth, farmers, women, workers and people from every section of society stand with PM Modi. PM Modi is going nowhere. He will return to the ramparts of the Red Fort in 2029. Rahul ji, keep dreaming! The youth, farmers, women, workers and every section of Indian society stand with PM Modi," he said.Nabin's Telangana visit was part of the BJP's 'Loktantra Bachao, Arajkata Hatao' campaign. The party has launched the campaign to counter what it describes as attempts by Congress and other opposition leaders, particularly Rahul Gandhi, to mislead people through fear, confusion and misinformation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

headline: Only BS-VI vehicles to ply in Delhi during winter: Supreme Court
content: The Supreme Court on Monday made it clear that only vehicles complying with BS-VI emission standards should be allowed to ply in Delhi during the pollution-prone winter months, even as it described the national capital’s relatively better air quality this November as a matter of good fortune, saying favourable winds had helped prevent the air quality from slipping into the severe category.“We are clear we will allow only BS-VI vehicles in Delhi, if not NCR,” a bench, comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, observed, signalling its intention to continue with restrictions on polluting vehicles during the winter months.The bench, which was hearing the Supreme Court’s ongoing suo motu proceedings on air pollution in Delhi-NCR, said it was “lucky” that the region had not experienced ‘severe’ category air pollution this November, attributing the relatively better conditions primarily to favourable meteorological conditions. “We have also been lucky this winter. There is no severe category pollution till now because of the winds,” it remarked.When additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), pointed to the efforts made by authorities to contain pollution, the court said: “Primarily nature.” Bhati maintained that enforcement measures had also contributed to the situation.The observations assume significance as the Delhi government has introduced restrictions on the entry and plying of vehicles that do not meet BS-VI emission standards during the winter months. Under its notification, vehicles registered outside Delhi that comply only with BS-IV or older emission norms are barred from plying in the capital between November 1 and January 31 every year.The Delhi government announced on November 7 that the restriction would be an annual measure, rather than a one-off intervention for the current winter. The prohibition covers BS-IV and older commercial goods vehicles, including light, medium and heavy goods vehicles, as well as buses entering the capital. CNG and electric vehicles are exempt, along with specified emergency and other exempted categories.The government has deployed enforcement personnel at major entry points, including DND, Rajokri on the Delhi-Jaipur highway, Ghazipur, Singhu, Tikri and Badarpur, to prevent violations. It has also said it is using special enforcement teams and automatic number plate recognition cameras to monitor compliance.The Supreme Court on Monday indicated that it is considering a more comprehensive approach to vehicular pollution, potentially extending restrictions beyond the existing framework and across the wider NCR.It also explored a five-year roadmap to progressively eliminate the entry of polluting commercial vehicles into Delhi without disrupting the supply of essential commodities. “Why not have this during five years? To ensure that no single commercial vehicle enters Delhi,” it suggested.It added that the idea should not be to prevent Delhi’s residents from accessing essential goods but to change the way these supplies are transported. “Why not how to ensure that commercial vehicles don’t enter Delhi at all? But it does not mean that Delhi people don’t require. They have a lot of necessities. They require vegetables, they require fruits, they need other day-to-day items,” the court observed.It suggested developing warehousing facilities at the city’s borders, where goods could be unloaded and subsequently transported into Delhi through battery-operated or other non-polluting vehicles. The bench acknowledged that such an arrangement might not be feasible immediately, or even next year, but said authorities should work towards putting it in place over the next five years.The court made it clear that the directions it eventually considers should not be confined to Delhi but should cover the entire NCR, where vehicular movement across state boundaries contributes to the region’s pollution burden.The focus on vehicular emissions comes against the backdrop of repeated judicial interventions and the continuing debate over the relative contribution of local and external sources to Delhi’s air pollution.The Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology’s Air Quality Early Warning System, in its source-apportionment estimates for November 23, attributed around 21.5% of Delhi’s PM2.5 pollution to transport within the city. It estimated that 60% of the particulate pollution load was from sources outside Delhi, underlining the need for coordinated action across the NCR and neighbouring states.The same estimates put the contribution from stubble burning at less than 1% on that day, although the contribution of crop-residue burning can vary considerably during the season.Favourable winds have played a role in preventing pollutants from accumulating close to the ground. The India Meteorological Department’s November 23 forecast indicated predominantly northwesterly winds over Delhi, with speeds reaching around 10 kmph during the afternoon. Such winds, along with a relatively deeper atmospheric mixing layer, help disperse pollutants instead of allowing them to remain trapped near the surface.The respite remains fragile. Delhi’s air quality has continued to fluctuate between the ‘poor’ and ‘very poor’ categories, with the CAQM having invoked Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan on November 6 after forecasting a possible deterioration into the severe category. The emergency measures were subsequently withdrawn on November 17 as air quality improved.The bench said it would examine what further short-term and long-term interventions were necessary to address the recurring pollution crisis. Senior advocate Aparajita Singh is assisting the court as amicus curiae.

headline: CPCB’s AQI method understates severity of Delhi’s worst pollution days | India News
content: India’s official air quality index has been underestimating how bad the air is on polluted days, because the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) seemingly does not follow the index’s own published definition when calculating it, according to CPCB documents and Delhi figures analysed by HT.HT ran the index’s calculations on a year of hourly readings from Delhi’s government monitoring stations and found that, scored by the index’s own definition, set out in at least four CPCB and government documents, the city would have been rated “severe” on 23 days, more than double the 10 that CPCB’s daily 4pm bulletins reported. The difference is starkest on the most polluted days.A stark example is this November, where HT’s calculations show Delhi’s air would have been “severe” on two days had the index been worked out as defined, while CPCB’s bulletins have yet to call a single day “severe”. No November since at least 2015 has gone without one, HT’s analysis of the bulletins shows, and November is usually the city’s most polluted month.The two days were Diwali, November 8, and the day after; CPCB’s bulletins called both “very poor”. On November 9, the index should have been 411 instead of the 344 CPCB published.Also Read: CAQM sets 15-20% pollution reduction target for Delhi-NCR in 2027, seeks district-wise action plans The undercount shows across the city’s monitors as well. On November 9, the day after Diwali, CPCB rated just one of Delhi’s monitoring stations “severe”, where 29 would have been “severe” had the definition been followed.“Nearly seventy points is almost a seventh of the whole scale, and it crosses the boundary that matters most,” said professor Gautam Menon of Ashoka University, of the gap on November 9.While HT’s analysis covers PM2.5 and PM10 in Delhi, on days when particulates were the main pollutants, the problem is not Delhi’s alone: CPCB’s published figures for more than 500 stations elsewhere in India are averaged from hourly scores in the same way, HT found. Also Read: Report links cloud-seeding to AQI gain in Delhi; but western disturbance may have had a roleTo be sure, CPCB’s practice makes cleaner days look slightly worse than they were, by less than 10 points, and it ranked Delhi in a worse category than it would have been in had the definition been followed, on only two days in the year. The error is far larger, and runs the other way, on the days when the air is most polluted.Why 24-hour average mattersTo understand the problem, it helps to first unpack what the index is meant to capture, and how it does it.The air quality index is a single number meant to reflect the dose of pollution a person takes in over a day, from fine particles to gases such as nitrogen dioxide, and to tell people what that dose means for their health.India defines the acceptable limit of exposure as a 24-hour average of 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5 -- the particles most harmful to human health and the kind that causes smog and haze. The World Health Organization advises a lower limit of 15µg/m³ -- Delhi’s “severe” days run far beyond both.Readings, methods and calculationsDelhi’s monitoring stations record each pollutant every hour. The index’s definition, laid out by CPCB and in the IIT Kanpur report that set up the index, requires each pollutant’s readings first to be averaged over 24 hours. That one average is then converted into a score, called a sub-index, using a fixed table, and the highest sub-index becomes the station’s AQI.HT found the same 24-hour average in five documents behind the index: three of CPCB’s own (its website note on the calculation, its AQI calculator and its November 10 clarification), the government’s 2009 notification of national air quality limits, and the 2014 report IIT Kanpur prepared for the expert group that set up the index. That report drew every band in terms of that 24-hour average and anchored the scale to the law: a score of 100, the top of the “satisfactory” band, matches India’s 24-hour legal limit for PM2.5.The index uses the average because the health effects of pollution are “believed to be largely cumulative”, said Menon, a physicist and biologist who models the spread of infectious disease. A day’s air could be summed up in other ways, by its worst hour, for instance, but the index was built to read the average -- the good hours and the bad.CPCB’s own documents describe this calculation. A note on its website, “How is AQI calculated?”, says the sub-index for each pollutant is “calculated using its 24-hourly average concentration value”. Its AQI calculator, a spreadsheet the board built for manual monitoring stations, scores a 24-hour average once, and in its clarification of November 10, 2026, issued to defend its Diwali figures, the board wrote that each pollutant’s sub-index “is calculated from its hourly average over the previous 24 hours”, and that the US Environmental Protection Agency follows a similar method.Where CPCB deviatesBut CPCB’s published numbers follow a different calculation. CPCB converts each hourly reading into a score separately, then publishes the average of the last 24 hourly scores as the AQI. CPCB’s live feed shows this: the score it posts each hour matches that one hour’s reading, not the day’s average.To corroborate this, HT scored each hour’s raw reading separately, the way CPCB scores each hour for its website, and averaged the 24 scores. The results matched CPCB’s station and city figures to within a fraction of a point. At R K Puram on Diwali night, for instance, averaging the 24 hourly scores gave 397, the figure CPCB showed at 11pm on November 8. Averaging the day’s PM2.5 readings first and converting that one average, as the definition says, gave 462, which is “severe”.The order matters because the index does not rise evenly. Low on the scale, a little more pollution pushes the score up a lot. High on the scale, a lot more pollution pushes it up only a little: an hour twice as smoky as a “very poor” hour scores only about a third higher.On a day when the air is bad all afternoon and far worse through the night, averaging the readings first lets the night hours pull the day’s figure up in full. But scoring each hour first marks those night hours down before they reach the average, and the day comes out cleaner than it was.On cleaner days, where the scale climbs faster, the effect reverses slightly.CPCB’s clarification says the US Environmental Protection Agency follows a similar method, but the EPA’s 2018 guidance on the AQI says that “it is not valid to use shorter-term (e.g. hourly) data to calculate an AQI value”.HT found no CPCB document that describes averaging hourly scores.The cap“Currently each band’s health meaning is attached to a 24-hour average concentration. Averaging hourly scores produces a different quantity. Because the scale flattens at high levels and stops at 500, the worst hours count for less,” Menon said.The worst hours worry him most: he said sharp spikes may matter far more for health than air that stays uniformly bad. CPCB’s practice discounts those hours twice over. It caps each hour’s score at the top of the scale, which a reading reaches at about 420 µg/m³, so an hour at 2,000 µg/m³ counts for no more than one at 420.But in its clarification of November 10, CPCB acknowledged for the first time that it also drops the worst hours altogether: readings above 1,000 µg/m³ “are not used in the computation”. On November 9, the day after Diwali, 12 stations were left out of the city’s figure for want of enough hours, and seven of them had readings above 1,000 µg/m³ blanked.The board’s explanation is that the analysers installed when the index was introduced were calibrated only up to 1,000 µg/m³, though it says instruments have advanced considerably since. The same statement says the index is meant to reflect “prolonged exposure, rather than a momentary reading”. Leaving out the worst hours strips the heaviest part of that exposure from the day’s average.For citizens, it means not just reading an undercount but getting used to it. “People can grow used to a number that tells them the air is less bad than it is,” Menon said.What is lostThe index’s bands come with health advice pitched at a day’s exposure in that range. When a “severe” day is published as “very poor”, people across the city are told to take less care than the air warrants.Averaging hourly scores also breaks the index’s link to the law. A score of 100 is meant to mark the legal limit for a day’s air, so a higher score shows how far past it the day went. An average of hourly scores no longer lines up with how polluted the day actually was, so it cannot show that.The undercount passes into the official record too, and HT could not establish how long the index has been computed this way.“If the method changed at an unknown date, comparisons across that date are unsafe,” Menon said. Health research is largely spared, he said, because Indian studies use measured or satellite-derived concentrations, not the published index.While the hours CPCB excludes pull the published figure lower still, so do the newer DPCC monitors, which an earlier HT investigation found read lower than the long-running network, even against older stations as far from the city centre.In effect, then, the AQI figures are weighed down in three ways: a calculation that does not follow the index’s own definition, a newly acknowledged practice of dropping readings when PM2.5 crosses 1,000 µg/m³, and newer monitors that read lower than the long-running network.CPCB’s note on the calculation says, in its fourth point, that the automated system “displays AQI based on running average values”, without saying whether it averages the readings or the scores. Read with the note’s first point, the natural interpretation is that it means the readings.HT’s analysis establishes how the published figures are calculated; the reason for the method is something only CPCB can explain, and the board did not respond to a questionnaire sent by HT.“The remedy is to publish the method and the hourly data so the record can be recomputed, though hours that were never recorded cannot be recovered,” Menon said.

headline: Delhi falls short on key pollution control steps | Latest News Delhi
content: Delhi has achieved several administrative and monitoring targets, but is falling significantly short on infrastructure-led pollution control, according to the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM)’s State Action Plan 2026 report card released on Sunday. Of 22 parameters, it achieved its targets on nine, including air-quality monitoring, construction and demolition waste processing capacity, industrial inspections and installation of pollution-control equipment. But significant gaps remain in tackling some of the city’s most persistent sources of pollution.The state-wise assessment of action plans for 2026 with progress recorded till October 31 also showed that Delhi may have performed better than its neighbouring National Capital Region states on several pollution-control measures.Pollution control targetsDelhi achieved its target of 19 continuous ambient air quality monitoring stations (CAAQMS), while Haryana had not achieved any of its target of 23 stations. Rajasthan had completed three of its five targets, while Uttar Pradesh had achieved 22 of 25.Delhi also achieved its target of 1,000 tonnes per day of construction and demolition (C&D) waste processing capacity, compared with 300 tonnes against a target of 400 tonnes in Uttar Pradesh and zero achievement against Haryana’s target of 115 tonnes.Also Read I Delhi traffic advisory for Nov 23: Restrictions in parts of Central, North Delhi amid VIP movement, Nagar KirtanThe Capital also completed 1,609 industrial inspections against a target of 979 and achieved its target of installing online continuous emission monitoring systems (OCEMS) and air pollution control devices at 90 industries. Haryana, meanwhile, completed just 177 of its 3,865 targeted industrial inspections, while Rajasthan completed 68 of 2,974 and Uttar Pradesh 730 of 3,789.However, government agencies lifted just 2.07 lakh metric tonnes against an annual target of 9.90 lakh tonnes, achieving 21% of the target. Private agencies lifted 3.08 lakh tonnes against a target of 12.09 lakh tonnes, or 26%. Delhi falls short on controlThe report also flags a major shortfall in municipal solid waste processing infrastructure. Delhi had targeted augmentation of two processing plants but reported no achievement till October-end. The targeted additional processing capacity of 650 tonnes per day also remained unachieved.The Capital’s three landfill sites continue to remain a major challenge. At Okhla, 18.26 lakh tonnes of legacy waste was cleared against a target of 27.45 lakh tonnes, while Bhalswa recorded 27.49 lakh tonnes against 48.42 lakh tonnes and Ghazipur 16.53 lakh tonnes against 39.12 lakh tonnes.Road dust management, another major contributor to Delhi’s pollution, presents a mixed picture. The city achieved its target of four small mechanical road sweeping machines, but had deployed only 19 of 35 large machines and just one of 57 medium-sized machines targeted for augmentation. Delhi also remained behind on vehicular pollution control. It added 1,703 city buses against a target of 2,395, achieving 71% of the target. While the target of 6,000 electric vehicle charging stations was achieved, only 15 of the 266 targeted parking lots had been developed.The report further shows that Delhi completed 34 of its 34 targeted short-term decongestion points but developed only eight of 28 long-term decongestion points. State-wise control measuresThe CAQM dashboard showed mixed progress across states in implementing measures to manage paddy stubble, a major contributor to air pollution in the Capital.While Haryana exceeded its annual target for functional Crop Residue Management (CRM) machines, with 13,700 machines against a target of 9,000, Punjab has achieved 19,890 against 22,500, or 88%. Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have also met their targets. However, Punjab continues to lag in setting up custom hiring centres, achieving 60% of its target of 632, while Rajasthan has achieved 53%. Uttar Pradesh has met its target of 41 centres, with 53 established.Punjab has also fallen short in creating bale storage infrastructure, achieving 860.5 hectares against a target of 1,016.76 hectares (85%), and in augmenting plant capacity, with 44 plants against a target of 72 (61%). In contrast, Haryana has exceeded its bale storage target, while Uttar Pradesh has achieved its and has 104 plants against a target of zero.Also Read I Delhi air stays 'poor' with AQI of 237; minimum temperature at 11.8°CSunil Dahiya, founder and lead analyst at the think tank Envirocatalysts, noted that more than half the ratings were unsatisfactory. “The report card measures effort, not air, all 29 indicators are inputs, and more than half the ratings are unsatisfactory, especially for industry inspections, buses and waste. Weather-adjusted, Delhi’s PM2.5 this year is no better than 2025. November was better, about 15% lower than last year on the same stations in broadly similar weather, which coincides with Stage III coming in earlier and CAQM’s 5–20 November curbs,” he added.

headline: 60% of Yamuna is totally clean, you can drink that water: Delhi Minister Sirsa
content: <p>New Delhi: Delhi Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa on Monday said 60 per cent of <a href="https://www.deccanherald.com/tags/yamuna">river Yamuna</a> has been cleaned, so much so that its water is now potable, and the entire river will be cleaned up by 2029 or 2030.</p>.<p>Speaking at the launch of Uber's "One Less Car" report here, the minister said the issue of vehicular pollution is a shared responsibility and even electric vehicles produce pollution, as their tyres lead to dust when moving.</p>.<p>Deliveries from cloud kitchens also add to pollution because of the number of workers and vehicles involved, he added.</p>.BJP to open 'Sheesh Mahal' for public viewing; attempt to divert attention from Yamuna froth, says AAP.<p>Sirsa credited Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and the Union government's support over the last two years for the cleaning of river Yamuna. He said work began at one end of the river and will move to the other, which is why 60 per cent is done and not the whole stretch.</p>.<p>"60 per cent of Yamuna ji is totally clean…Clean means so clean that you can (even) drink that water," he said, urging people to visit the river and see for themselves.</p>.<p>Sirsa said the city's sewage goes through drains into the Yamuna, and a clean river is impossible unless that sewage is treated. He said the government is using sewage treatment plants (STPs) to deal with the issue.</p>.'Can no longer hide behind data': Supreme Court warns states, union territories of penalties over Yamuna pollution.<p>Earlier this month, <a href="https://www.deccanherald.com/tags/supreme-court">the Supreme Court of India </a>said pollution in Yamuna has only increased despite huge sums being spent on cleaning the river, directing the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) to monitor water quality at the points where the Yamuna and its major drains enter and exit states, union territories and districts.</p>.<p>In an order dated November 4, a bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Manmohan observed that industrial pollutants and untreated sewage must be stopped at the source, and merely constructing more sewage treatment plants is not sufficient to clean the river.</p>.<p>"This court is of the opinion that everything that is wrong with the civic administration in towns, cities and villages situated along the banks of the river is reflected in the poor health of the river and in the 520 drains that discharge waste water into the Yamuna.</p>.<p>"This is why, despite huge sums being spent on cleaning the river, pollution in the Yamuna has only increased," the bench said while hearing a plea related to cleaning of the river.</p>.<p>On the city's garbage, Sirsa said 60 per cent of the legacy waste of the last 25 years has been cleared in less than two years, with support from the Union government. "Coming generations will see garbage mountains only in pictures, not in real life," he said.</p>.Delhi air pollution: CAQM directs district-level action plans for 2027 to reduce AQI by 15-20% .<p>Turning to <a href="https://www.deccanherald.com/tags/air-pollution">air pollution</a>, the minister said it is not one person's responsibility and called for public participation, saying the government alone cannot ensure clean air.</p>.<p>"Nothing is more important than health. Nothing is more important than clean air," he said.</p>.<p>Sirsa said the city has seen improvement this year and that more days in October and the first half of November were clean than in earlier years. Citing a New York Times article, he said the area around Delhi University recorded an air quality index of 900 in 2012.</p>.<p>No vehicle below the Bharat Stage-VI emission standard, including heavy vehicles and buses, is now allowed to enter Delhi from neighbouring areas of the National Capital Region, Sirsa said. </p>

headline: Order cancelling UK-based journalist's OCI card lacks specific reasons: Delhi High Court
content: <p>New Delhi: The Delhi High Court has said that the Centre’s show-cause notice and order cancelling the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card of UK-based journalist of Indian origin Amrit Wilson did not specify her alleged anti-India activities, and directed the authorities to issue a fresh notice detailing the grounds for cancellation.</p>.<p>Justice Amit Mahajan passed the order on a petition filed by Wilson challenging the Centre’s 2023 decision to cancel her OCI card.</p>.<p>In an order passed on November 19, the court directed the authorities to issue a fresh show-cause notice with specific details within one week and allowed Wilson another week to respond. The authorities would then pass an order within two weeks, it said.</p>.<p>The court, however, clarified that the existing cancellation order would remain in operation for four weeks or until a fresh order was passed, whichever was earlier.</p>.Guidelines issued during anti-CEC protest to distinguish journalists from reel-makers, Delhi police tell Supreme Court.<p>It observed that in the absence of specific details, Wilson had not been given an opportunity to explain her position, and even the Centre’s reply to her petition lacked specific reasons.</p>.<p>“A perusal of the SCN and the impugned order indicates that the same is bereft of any specific details of anti-India activities in which the petitioner was involved, thus providing no opportunity to the petitioner to provide an explanation in respect of the same. In the given facts, this Court is of the view that principles of natural justice have not been followed,” the court said.</p>.<p>“The rights of the petitioner under Section 7B of the (Citizenship) Act cannot be taken without providing an appropriate opportunity to the petitioner to respond to the allegations against her,” it held.</p>.<p>Section 7B of the Citizenship Act deals with the rights conferred on OCI cardholders.</p>.<p>The court also said that if the authorities were unable to spell out specific reasons in the fresh notice, they should provide Wilson with the “gist of the material while redacting the sensitive part of the information” or allow her to inspect the relevant material.</p>.<p>The Centre had cancelled Wilson’s OCI card in 2023, alleging that she had engaged in “detrimental propaganda against the Indian government”.</p>.<p>In her petition, Wilson contended that the March 17, 2023 order cancelling her OCI card was ex facie illegal and arbitrary. She alleged that it had been passed by the Indian High Commission in London mechanically, without application of mind and in violation of the principles of natural justice.</p>.<p>The High Commission had issued a show-cause notice to Wilson in November 2022, accusing her of being “engaged in detrimental propaganda against the Indian government” and involved in “multiple anti-India activities” that posed a threat to the sovereignty and integrity of India and the interests of the general public.</p>.<p>Wilson argued that the notice was arbitrary as it did not provide any material particulars or a summary of specific reasons to substantiate the allegations against her.</p>.<p>Wilson, who was born in India, surrendered her Indian passport and acquired British citizenship in 2009.</p>
