headline: Delhi minister Sirsa claims 60% of Yamuna cleaned, says entire river will be clean by 2030
content: Delhi Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa on Monday claimed that 60 per cent of the Yamuna has been cleaned and its water is now fit for drinking, adding that the entire river would be cleaned by 2029-30.Speaking at the launch of Uber's 'One Less Car' report in Delhi, Sirsa credited Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and the Centre's support for the progress made over the past two years. He said the cleaning work was being carried out in phases, starting from one end of the river and gradually extending to the remaining stretches."60 per cent of Yamuna ji is totally clean… Clean means so clean that you can (even) drink that water," he said, urging people to visit the river and assess its condition.Sirsa said untreated sewage flowing through drains into the Yamuna remained a major challenge, adding that the government was using sewage treatment plants (STPs) to address the problem.His remarks come against the backdrop of the Supreme Court's recent observations that pollution in the Yamuna had increased despite substantial expenditure on its cleaning..SC warns states, UTs of penalties as pollution in Yamuna worsens. In an order dated November 4, a bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Manmohan directed the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) to monitor water quality at points where the river and its major drains enter and exit states, Union Territories and districts.The court said industrial pollutants and untreated sewage must be intercepted at source, observing that merely constructing more STPs would not be enough to clean the river.It also noted that the poor state of civic administration in settlements along the river was reflected in its deteriorating health, with 520 drains discharging wastewater into the Yamuna.On Delhi's waste management, Sirsa claimed that 60 per cent of the legacy waste accumulated over 25 years had been cleared in less than two years with the Centre's support. He said future generations would see the city's garbage mountains only in photographs.Addressing air pollution, the minister said tackling the problem required collective responsibility and public participation, adding that the government alone could not ensure clean air.He claimed that Delhi had recorded more clean-air days in October and the first half of November this year compared with previous years. Referring to a New York Times article, he also cited an air quality index (AQI) reading of 900 recorded near Delhi University in 2012.Sirsa further said vehicles that do not meet Bharat Stage-VI emission standards, including heavy vehicles and buses, were no longer allowed to enter Delhi from neighbouring areas of the National Capital Region.Speaking about vehicular emissions, he said pollution was not limited to conventional fuel-powered vehicles, as electric vehicles also contributed to dust pollution through tyre movement. Deliveries from cloud kitchens also added to pollution due to the large number of delivery workers and vehicles involved."Nothing is more important than health. Nothing is more important than clean air," he said.(With inputs from PTI).Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: SC seeks response of Centre, EC on PIL for reforms in anti-defection law
content: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday sought responses from the Centre, the Election Commission and the Law Commission on a PIL seeking comprehensive reforms in the anti-defection framework.The PIL raised concerns over alleged misuse of resignations by elected representatives to circumvent disqualification proceedings and influence the survival of elected governments.Besides the Election Commission and the law panel, a bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also issued notices to the Ministries of Law and Justice and Parliamentary Affairs on the PIL filed by one A Sethu.The PIL, filed through lawyers R Satish Kumar and Jatin, sought directions to prevent misuse of “strategic resignations” by MPs and lawmakers from legislative assemblies to evade discipline of the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution.It also sought directions to “(ii) secure time-bound, reasoned and transparent adjudication of resignations and disqualification proceedings; (iii) secure institutional review of the Speaker-centred adjudicatory mechanism; and (iv) reaffirm that in a hung Legislative Assembly, majority to form the Government must be tested only on the floor of a duly constituted House after Members are sworn under Article 188, and not through extra-parliamentary letters of support or demonstrations.”The plea said that legislators facing, or anticipating, disqualification proceedings frequently resort to strategic resignations before the Speaker or Chairman can decide the cases on merit..The plea said such resignations can be used to facilitate political realignments, alter the numerical strength of legislative assemblies and potentially enable elected representatives to evade the consequences contemplated under the anti-defection law.“Declare and direct that a resignation tendered by a Member of Parliament or a Member of a State Legislative Assembly, at a stage when disqualification proceedings under the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution are pending or reasonably imminent against such member, shall not ipso facto terminate or render infructuous such disqualification proceedings, and that the Speaker/Chairman shall record a reasoned order, based on objective material, on both the voluntariness and genuineness of the resignation and on the disqualification petition,” the plea said.The plea sought direction to Speakers and Chairpersons to examine the voluntariness and genuineness of resignations on the basis of objective material and pass reasoned orders, while ensuring that pending disqualification proceedings are independently adjudicated.(With inputs from PTI).Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: Delhi AQI Remains ‘Poor’ at 249; Punjabi Bagh Most Polluted at 282
content: New Delhi: Delhi continued to grapple with poor air quality on Monday morning, with the national capital recording an overall Air Quality Index (AQI) of 249 at 8 am. Punjabi Bagh emerged as the most polluted among the listed monitoring stations, recording an AQI of 282, according to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).According to the CPCB, Punjabi Bagh recorded the highest AQI, followed by Bawana at 273 and Chandni Chowk at 271. All three stations fell in the 'poor' category.Meanwhile, Anand Vihar (237), Ashok Vihar (240), Narela (239), Okhla Phase 2 (213), Rohini (252), Sonia Vihar (215), Patparganj (208), Mandir Marg (225), Major Dhyan Chand Stadium (202), Alipur (246), IGI Airport Terminal 3 (217) and RK Puram (252) also recorded air quality in the 'poor' category.However, Vasundhara Enclave recorded a relatively better AQI of 170, placing it in the 'moderate' category.According to the CPCB classification, an AQI between 0 and 50 is considered 'good', 51-100 'satisfactory', 101-200 'moderate', 201-300 'poor', 301-400 'very poor' and 401-500 'severe'.Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast mainly clear skies across Delhi-NCR over the next five days, with mist and shallow fog likely during morning hours on November 23 and 24.The district-wise forecast, issued by the Regional Meteorological Centre, New Delhi, on November 22, indicates that similar weather conditions are expected across all districts of Delhi, including North, South, East, West, Central and New Delhi, as well as neighbouring areas such as Noida, Ghaziabad, Gurugram and Faridabad.The IMD has further forecast mist and shallow fog at many places across the region on November 25 and 26, with moderate fog likely at isolated places on November 25 and a few places on November 26 during morning hours.The forecast suggests that foggy conditions could become more widespread towards the end of the five-day period, potentially affecting morning visibility across parts of Delhi-NCR.Earlier on Sunday, the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) began assessing and ranking Delhi and neighbouring states on their performance in implementing measures to combat air pollution.Its 2026 report card, covering progress up to October, highlighted significant gaps across several key areas, including industrial inspections, waste management, public transport and pollution-monitoring infrastructure.According to the State Action Plan-2026 report card, none of the four states and Delhi have established the targeted number of green crematoriums.Against a combined target of 421 green crematoriums across Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, the achievement stood at zero as of October 31.The report card has been prepared based on progress recorded up to October 2026. The final report card for the year is scheduled to be released in January 2027, allowing the states and the Delhi government to improve their performance by accelerating the implementation of pollution-control measures during the remaining period of the year.The CAQM has classified performance of 100 per cent as satisfactory, achievement between 75 per cent and less than 100 per cent as needing improvement, and progress below 75 per cent as unsatisfactory.Among the key areas flagged, industrial inspections recorded particularly poor progress in three states.Against a combined annual target of 11,607 inspections in Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, only 2,584 inspections had been completed by October 31, leaving a gap of 9,023.Delhi exceeded its target, conducting 1,609 inspections against 979. However, Haryana completed only 177 of its 3,865 targeted inspections, while Rajasthan recorded 68 against 2,974 and Uttar Pradesh 730 against 3,789.The CAQM report card provides a review of the implementation of pollution-control measures under the State Action Plan-2026. The final assessment in January 2027 will reflect the progress made by the states and the Delhi government during the remaining period of the year.

headline: Pak minister seeks India's invitation for talks on Indus Waters Treaty, avoids questions on past threat
content: Pakistan's Climate Change and Environmental Coordination Minister Musadik Masood Malik on Sunday said he would discuss the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) with India if New Delhi extended a formal invitation for bilateral talks, when questioned about his earlier remarks threatening action over the suspension of the water-sharing agreement.Malik, who is leading Pakistan's delegation at the first Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi, was asked about the treaty, which India placed in abeyance following the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack."When you invite me to discuss the Indus Water Treaty, we will certainly talk about it. You haven't invited me to discuss the Indus Water Treaty at this moment," he said.Asked about his earlier statements on the issue, Malik said he would respond to questions on specific bilateral matters if India initiated a formal dialogue."When you invite me to discuss those specific issues, I shall be there. But first, you must extend that invitation. Tell me that you wish to engage in a bilateral dialogue; when you invite me for such a discussion, I will be present, and I will then answer all the bilateral questions you choose to ask," he said..Malik's remarks came months after he criticised India's decision to place the 1960 treaty in abeyance. In June, he had warned that Pakistan would "cut off that hand" which attempted to take away its share of water, while accusing New Delhi of using water as a means of exerting pressure on Islamabad.India has maintained that its position on the treaty remains unchanged. On Friday, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal reiterated New Delhi's stand when asked about Malik's visit and his earlier remarks."As far as the IWT is concerned, we have made our position very clear and that is where it remains. There is absolutely no change," Jaiswal said.India placed the treaty in abeyance after the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir, in which 26 people were killed. New Delhi has said the decision will remain in force until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism.The suspension followed Operation Sindoor, launched by India in response to the Pahalgam attack. The operation targeted terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Military exchanges between the two countries continued until a ceasefire understanding was reached on May 10, 2025.The Indus Waters Treaty, signed in 1960, governs the sharing of the Indus river system between India and Pakistan. The river system is crucial to Pakistan's agriculture and water supply, with a large share of its agricultural land and water use dependent on its waters.Malik's visit to New Delhi for the November 20-22 SCO forum marks a rare visit by a Pakistani federal minister to India amid strained bilateral relations. India had invited all SCO member countries, including Pakistan, to participate in the multilateral event.(With inputs from ANI).Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: Pak minister Malik, wife explore Delhi
content: Finding some personal time from his busy schedule at the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, Pakistan’s federal minister Musadik Malik, along with his wife, visited the historic Qutub Minar and explored other sites in Delhi.Union Culture Secretary Vivek Aggarwal said this in response to a query during a press conference on the closing day of the Forum hosted at the historic Purana Quila from November 20-22. The three-day forum at the Purana Quila was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 20. It saw the participation of delegates from various Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) member countries and other countries.Qutub Minar is a centrally protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) and one of the three UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Delhi, the other two being the Red Fort and Humayun’s Tomb.Asked if any formal bilateral talks were held between India and Pakistan on the sidelines, Aggarwal said, “There were no formal bilateral talks between the two sides.” However, he said that members of the Indian side did have interactions with him over banquets and during the conference, as well as other “informal discussions” with him during the course of the forum, as with other ministers too.Asked about reports claiming that the Pakistan minister wanted to visit the Taj Mahal and the Nizamuddin area, but couldn’t, the secretary said, “I do not have an idea if there is an issue related to permission, but this matter has not come to me.”“However, he is visiting the Qutub Minar, and he will also see exhibitions put up here (at Purana Quila). We have given him a liaison officer, and he and his wife are exploring Delhi well, and going to various monuments and various sites,” Aggarwal said, while interacting with reporters shortly before the closing session in the evening.

headline: Former Minister Harsh Vardhan stresses early diagnosis for cancer
content: Former Union Health Minister Harsh Vardhan on Sunday stressed the need for early diagnosis to improve cancer treatment outcomes. He was speaking as chief guest at the inauguration of M|O|C Cancer Care & Research Centre in Delhi at New Delhi.“Cancer is an important public health concern. Timely diagnosis can significantly influence treatment outcomes, making access to screening, medical advice and specialised facilities especially important,” Dr Vardhan said. He said centres can bridge gaps in access by bringing dedicated cancer care closer to people’s homes. “The centre is equipped to support patients across different stages of their treatment, with chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy and access to advanced treatment pathways,” Dr Sachita Pal said.According to ICMR estimates, Delhi’s cancer burden increased by approximately 12.6 per cent between 2021 and 2025.

headline: Can fuel be ethanol-blended without hurting India’s food security?
content: India’s attainment of 20 per cent ethanol blending in petrol (E20) in 2025-26, five years ahead of the 2030 deadline, is commendable. But sustaining it depends on ensuring ample supplies of feedstocks without jeopardising food security. Growing reliance on foodgrains in Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2026-27 has revived the food-versus-fuel debate. Due to tight sugar supplies, record prices and a weak monsoon in Maharashtra and Karnataka, the Centre has rightly directed oil marketing companies (OMCs) to cut sugar diversion for ethanol to zero. Their October tender excludes ethanol from cane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses, retaining only C-heavy molasses. This protects sugar availability for consumers but increases grain dependence for ethanol. Launched in 2003 with 5 per cent blending in nine states and four UTs, the Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme spent its first decade constrained by thin, sugar-dependent supplies. Administered prices, assured OMC offtake and the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018, which admitted maize and surplus foodgrains, lifted blending from about 5 per cent in 2019-20 to 20 per cent in 2025-26. The question is no longer whether India can produce enough ethanol, but from what, and at whose expense. Rice and maize account for almost all of this shift. FCI rice entered the mix in 2020-21 with under 1 per cent of supply, reached 13.5 per cent by ESY25 despite a near-halt in 2023-24, and accounts for 44 per cent of ESY27 allocations. Ethanol allocations from damaged foodgrains rose 164 per cent over ESY26, raising concerns about storage-related quality losses. Maize’s share increased from 6 per cent in ESY23 to 47 per cent in ESY27. It is also the mainstay of poultry feed and, increasingly, of dairy feed and starch. Mandi prices have already reached Rs 2,800 per quintal (Agmarknet), well above the MSP of Rs 2,400 per quintal. Either distillers bid maize prices higher, passing the cost on to poultry farmers and milk consumers, or they fall short of their commitments, putting E20 itself at risk. The growing use of rice as ethanol feedstock carries substantial fiscal and environmental costs. FCI holds 39 MMT of rice and 20.27 MMT in rice-equivalent paddy stocks, more than five times the October 1 buffer norm. Rice allocations for ethanol rose from 3.11 MMT in ESY25 to an initial estimate of 7.2 MMT in ESY27. The latest ESY27 allocation of 483.8 crore litres of rice-based ethanol, comprising 159.9 crore litres from damaged rice and 323.9 crore litres from surplus rice, implies roughly 11.2 MMT of rice, using conversion factors of 2.5 and 2.22 kg per litre of ethanol, respectively (NITI Aayog, 2021). The fiscal disparity is stark. FCI sells rice to distilleries at Rs 23.20 per kg, 47 per cent below its economic cost of Rs 43.91 per kg. ICRIER (2024) research shows that rice production in the Punjab-Haryana belt gets roughly Rs 10 as power and fertiliser subsidy per kg of rice. This means that the real economic cost of rice is nearly Rs 53.91 The Department of Food estimates that it takes 2.5-3 kg of rice per litre of ethanol. Assuming an average conversion rate of 2.75 kg of rice per litre of ethanol, each litre of ethanol embodies Rs 148 in public expenditure. Interestingly, the price of ethanol paid by OMCs is only Rs 60.32 That means that OMCs get an indirect subsidy of Rs 87.93 per litre of ethanol produced from rice. Applied to 11.2 MMT of rice allocated for ethanol, this implies a fiscal cost of more than Rs 35,800 crore to the exchequer. The environmental costs are equally alarming. In March 2026, the Petroleum Ministry informed Parliament that rice was the most water-intensive ethanol feedstock. At 2.75 kg of rice per litre of ethanol, and 4,000 litres of irrigation water required per kg of rice, each litre of ethanol embodies 11,000 litres of irrigation water. For 11.2 MMT of rice, this implies a potential water footprint of 44.8 billion cubic metres. Flooded paddy also generates methane emissions. ICRIER research estimates it at 5 tonnes CO₂e per hectare in the Punjab-Haryana belt (Singh and Gulati, 2025). In contrast, rainfed kharif maize requires one-fifth as much irrigation water as rice and generates much lower methane emissions. Three key measures could help strengthen the programme. The first is a systematic study of the optimal supply and usage of feedstocks. A feedstock-specific, well-to-wheel assessment, benchmarked against the landed cost of imported ethanol, should guide procurement prices and allocations, replacing ad hoc adjustments. Second, the E20 mandate should be flexible. A dynamic blending band of E15-E20, tied to pre-announced triggers based on sugar output, grain stocks and maize prices, would allow the programme to contract in deficit years and expand in surplus ones, with ethanol imports as a safety valve. Third, diversification beyond first-generation food and feedstocks towards second- and third-generation alternatives is essential. The Pradhan Mantri Jaiv Indhan-Vatavaran Anukool Fasal Awashesh Nivaran (PM JI-VAN) Yojana, extended to 2028-29, supports ethanol from crop residues, industrial waste and algae, yet second-generation plants remain few and paddy straw is still burnt rather than distilled. Seaweed offers a third-generation option requiring no farmland, fertiliser or irrigation. Though yields are not yet commercially viable, targeted research and pilot coastal biorefineries could produce a genuinely green fuel that competes with neither food nor groundwater. The food-versus-fuel debate is not new. For a country of about 1.48 billion people, which also feeds one of the world’s largest livestock populations, it carries particular weight. Ethanol blending can reduce dependence on imported oil, but its gains must be weighed against pressures on food and feed security, groundwater depletion and the environmental costs of water-intensive crops. India has demonstrated its ability to scale up ethanol blending. The next challenge is to sustain that without compromising food security or environmental sustainability. Gulati is distinguished professor and Das is fellow at ICRIER. Views are personal

headline: MLAs walk out as paddy procurement committee sparks row
