headline: Fatal paragliding accidents at Bir-Billing threaten Himachal’s adventure tourism, deter foreign pilots
content: A spate of fatal paragliding accidents at Bir-Billing in Kangra district and various flying sites in Kullu has emerged as a major setback to Himachal Pradesh’s adventure tourism industry. Repeated mishaps, the alleged involvement of inexperienced pilots and the failure of regulatory agencies to enforce safety norms have raised serious concerns among tourists and professional paragliders. Foreign pilots, in particular, are increasingly reluctant to visit Bir-Billing.The economic implications are considerable. A foreign paragliding pilot visiting Bir-Billing spends over $20,000 during a stay on hotel accommodation, local transportation, taxi services, food, equipment-related services and other tourism activities. Such visitors generate business for a wide network of local service providers and contribute significantly to the region’s tourism economy. Any decline in their visits could, therefore, affect hotels, homestays, taxi operators, restaurants and other small businesses.The growing number of accidents has not only raised questions about the safety of tandem flying but also threatened the international reputation of Bir-Billing, regarded as one of the world’s premier paragliding destinations. A decline in foreign participation could affect international events, tourism-related businesses and the livelihoods of hundreds of people associated with the sector.With Bir-Billing attracting domestic and international visitors, the state government needs to treat the issue as a matter of tourism policy and public safety. Regular verification of pilot licences, mandatory equipment inspections, insurance checks, weather monitoring and strict action against violations are urgently required.Tourism stakeholders fear that unless the government restores confidence through a credible safety mechanism, repeated accidents could damage Himachal Pradesh’s image as a leading adventure tourism destination. The state cannot afford to lose international pilots and high-spending tourists because of inadequate safety arrangements and poor enforcement of regulations.Naveen Sareen, who introduced paragliding at Billing in 1990, said flying in challenging high-altitude terrain, such as the Dhauladhar ranges and the Kullu valley, required considerable experience and sound knowledge of local topography. He said several accidents had occurred because pilots lacked adequate knowledge of the terrain and changing flying conditions.The absence of a permanent, well-equipped rescue mechanism, effective weather monitoring and strict supervision has also remained a major concern.The situation at Bir-Billing is equally disturbing. During the past five years, 20 persons, including six tourists, have reportedly lost their lives in paragliding accidents in the region. Despite these fatalities, questions remain over the effectiveness of departmental inquiries and follow-up action against pilots allegedly responsible for the accidents. The failure to take stringent action, including the suspension or cancellation of licences, has further exposed weaknesses in the regulatory system.Information gathered by The Tribune suggests that several pilots involved in accidents in recent years allegedly lacked adequate flying experience and had incomplete documentation. The failure of regulatory agencies to regularly verify pilot licences, flying hours, equipment and insurance coverage has aggravated the situation.There are also complaints that some pilots overcharge tourists and violate prescribed operating norms. Several pilots have reportedly failed to maintain the mandatory dual insurance cover required under state regulations, raising concerns about the financial protection available to accident victims and their families.

headline: Cement prices set to rise further as Himachal Pradesh adds new clinker cess
content: The Himachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly’s passage of the Himachal Pradesh Taxation (On Certain Goods Carried by Road) Amendment Bill, 2026, has triggered fresh concerns over a further increase in cement prices in the state. The proposed amendment introduces an environmental cess of up to Rs 25 per tonne on clinker transported outside Himachal Pradesh by road. Cement manufacturers fear that once the Bill is notified as an Act, the additional levy will push up production costs and eventually be passed on to consumers.High cement prices in Himachal Pradesh, despite the presence of major manufacturers such as Adani Cement and UltraTech, which operate six manufacturing plants in Solan and Bilaspur districts, have remained a contentious issue. With cement being one of the most widely consumed construction materials, successive state-level levies have made it a significant source of revenue for the government, while consumers continue to bear the burden of rising prices.The introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in July 2017 was intended to create a unified, destination-based indirect tax regime by subsuming several central and state levies. However, Himachal Pradesh continues to impose the Certain Goods Carried by Road (CGCR) tax on cement and its raw materials, including clinker and limestone, adding to the tax burden on the industry.The impact of these levies became particularly evident after the Centre reduced GST on cement from 28 per cent to 18 per cent with effect from September 22, following the GST Council’s recommendation. Consumers in Himachal Pradesh, however, could not fully benefit from the reduction as the state government increased the CGCR levy from Rs 11 to Rs 16 per 50-kg bag on September 24, within two days of the GST cut, citing the need to offset revenue losses.The CGCR has witnessed successive increases over the past few years. According to an Adani Cement official, the levy on cement, which earlier stood at Rs 150 per tonne, was increased to Rs 220 per tonne in September 2023, raising the plant’s annual input costs by Rs 37 crore. A further hike to Rs 320 per tonne in September 2025 added another Rs 53 crore to the manufacturing cost.The burden has also extended to clinker, the principal intermediate ingredient in Portland cement. The CGCR on clinker was increased from Rs 120 to Rs 130 per tonne in March 2026, adding another Rs 5 crore to manufacturing costs, the official said.Electricity, another major input in cement production, has also become more expensive. In September 2023, the state government raised electricity duty on cement manufacturing from 17 to 25 per cent, making it the highest among industries. The discontinuation of the Rs 1-per-unit electricity subsidy for industrial consumers from October 1, 2024, further imposed an annual burden of around Rs 5 crore on manufacturers.The government subsequently introduced additional levies, including milk cess and environment cess of 10 paise each on electricity charges from November 16, 2024. These measures have added an estimated Rs 10 crore annually to the industry’s costs, which manufacturers say are ultimately passed on to consumers.Apart from taxation, high transportation costs have compounded the problem, with freight rates reportedly touching Rs 10.50 per tonne per kilometre. The widening price gap with neighbouring states reflects the impact of these additional costs. A 50-kg bag of cement reportedly sells for around Rs 430 in Solan and other bordering areas of Himachal Pradesh, compared with as little as Rs 370 in neighbouring Punjab and Haryana.Manufacturers fear that the proposed environmental cess on clinker will further widen this gap. Preliminary estimates by the industry suggest that even a Rs 10-per-tonne increase in the clinker levy could translate into an additional annual manufacturing cost of Rs 8 crore to Rs 10 crore.Clinker, transported by manufacturers from Darlaghat to cement grinding units within and outside the state, is ground with a small quantity of gypsum to produce finished cement. Any additional tax on its transportation, therefore, is likely to raise production costs and put further pressure on cement prices.With construction and housing projects already facing rising input costs, the latest proposed levy has once again brought the state’s taxation policy under scrutiny, particularly over its impact on the affordability of an essential building material.

headline: In crime and punishment, inclusion and exclusion, who is a ‘woman’?
content: By Shivani Vij While the challenge to the Transgender (Amendment) Act, 2026 remains pending in the Supreme Court, a related but distinct question has surfaced before the courts: Does the word “woman” in penal statutes include a transgender woman, or is its application confined to a cisgender woman? The constitutional recognition of gender identity in NALSA v. UOI (2014) favours inclusivity, but the issue is more nuanced and is best addressed in two categories. Although the courts are yet to settle the question conclusively, there is a case for inclusion under both. In a recent case concerning outraging modesty under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bombay High Court interpreted the pre-amendment definition and held that the allegations could be sustained by a transgender person who identifies as a woman (Vishal Sunil Ingle, 2026). Her self-identification could not be questioned at the stage of the discharge of the accused. The complainant had been receiving hormonal treatment for several years and dressed as a woman, although she had not undergone gender-affirming surgery. The Court also ruled in favour of a transgender woman who had undergone surgery and married thereafter, by including her as an “aggrieved person” under the Domestic Violence Act, on the basis that it was not restricted to the binary of women and men (Vithal Manik Khatri, 2023). The Andhra Pradesh High Court adopted a similar approach and held that a transgender woman living in a heterosexual marriage could invoke provisions on cruelty (Vishwanathan Krishna Murthy, 2025). Also Read | Proposed changes to Transgender Persons Act turn back the clock on rights and dignity Allahabad, however, interpreted it narrowly. In the context of false promise to marry, the Allahabad High Court held that despite undergoing gender-affirming surgery, transgender women do not fall under the statutory definition of a woman and cannot claim the protection of penal laws. It distinguished transgender from cisgender women and stated that the law intended for them to be protected separately, retaining the distinction between sex and gender (Mohd Saakir 2026). The Himachal Pradesh High Court took a similar view. When gender identity conforms to sex Leaving aside the amendment, which narrows the definition of a transgender person, Section 7(1) recognises a transgender person’s choice to undergo gender-affirming surgery. Having done so, the person is eligible for a change in the legal recognition of their gender, which now conforms to their sex (Section 7(3)), resulting in a change in their identity documents. Once this choice is made, there is little justification for excluding transgender women from the statutory protections available to women merely because their female sex characteristics were acquired through medical intervention rather than present at birth. Such exclusion is irrational and arbitrary under Article 14. They are entitled to the full protection of laws that penalise crimes against women and other benefits available to cisgender women, in addition to the ones under the Transgender Act (proviso, Section 7(3)). This category is largely non-contentious and therefore makes an easy case for inclusion. When gender identity does not conform to sex Transgender persons who have not chosen gender-affirming surgery include persons with intersex variations at birth, as per the amended definition, and also persons with a self-perceived gender identity, as per the original definition under Section 2(k). Their exclusion, based on the ground that they do not possess some or all biological characteristics conventionally associated with females, undermines their right to gender identity, which is a substantive protection of autonomy and freedom from violence, not contingent upon surgery. First, although the legislature enacted the Transgender Act in 2019 and granted protections in the form of non-discrimination and welfare, it framed only piecemeal offences for crimes against transpersons, such as abuse, coercion and exploitation. These offences carry a punishment of a maximum of two years (Section 18), far less than those against women under BNS. The legislative response has been lukewarm and left a complete vacuum as far as sexual and gender-based violence against transgender women is concerned. This itself provides a strong basis for inclusion. Second, persons with intersex variations who identify as women, and persons whose self-perceived gender identity is female, face numerous disadvantages arising from such identification. This does not mean that the disadvantages faced by cisgender and transgender women are always similar, or that the inclusion of the latter should depend on a similar disadvantage. It simply means that the discrimination arises from their identification with the feminine gender. Thus, biological characteristics cannot be the sole determinant of legal protection. Third, the true test should be whether the ingredients of an offence are otherwise satisfied under the penal statute. If they are, the class of victims should be read broadly. Where a trans woman is subjected to non-consensual sexual acts falling within the physical acts under the definition of rape, protection should not be denied solely because the sex assigned at birth disqualifies her as a victim. This would also make a case for gender-neutral sexual offences through a broader legislative reform, but that would be a separate conversation. While the question would ultimately require consideration by the Supreme Court, it must be an interpretation that favours inclusion rather than exclusion. This would not prevent the legislature from enacting special provisions for aggravated crimes but would acknowledge the recognition and inclusion that transgender women have long been fighting for. The writer is Advocate-on-Record, Supreme Court of India

headline: For Bihar teen forced into labour and left disabled, the road to justice is 1,400 km long
content: Swimming in the Ratwa River, looking after the family’s cows, and staying close to his home in Bihar's Kishanganj – the 16-year-old boy only wants to return to the simple pleasures of village life. But nowadays, home offers only a temporary respite. The teen is still living with the consequences of what happened after he left home a year ago in search of work. Held captive at a farm in Uttar Pradesh, he was thrashed, made to work long hours, and was abandoned in a forest after he lost an arm in an accident involving a fodder-cutting machine. Back in Bihar now, he has to repeatedly travel over 1,400 km to attend court hearings in Haryana – where he was found – and recount the trauma he has been struggling to forget. In a hotel room, the teenager sits on the edge of the bed, dressed in a beige printed T-shirt and navy trousers. A black stole rests across his shoulders. His father, Bhimlal Rishidev, 58, sits beside him in a red striped shirt. They have travelled from Khurkhuria village in Bihar's Kishanganj district for a court hearing in Jhajjar, Haryana. The minor gestures with his right hand as he speaks. His father listens. There are moments when Bhimlal sits quietly behind him, letting his son speak. The teenager is less concerned about his journey or the money it has cost. What troubles him is something else – he can’t understand why the man he trusted treated him the way he did. “Unhone itna galat kyu kiya hamare samjh me nahi aata aaj tak. Humne unka kya bigada tha? (To this day, I am unable to understand why he wronged me. What did I do to him?),” he asks. The minor was just 15 when he was allegedly taken to the dairy farm in Gautam Buddha Nagar. He says he was promised food, water and a monthly wage but, instead, was made to work long hours, beaten up, and kept away from his family. Today, he is back in his village, but with the case being heard in Haryana, he is required to travel back for the proceedings. His father says the family has spent more than Rs 25,000 on the latest trip, flying from the nearest airport in Siliguri to New Delhi. Their village is around 50-60 km from the Kishanganj district headquarters and the train journey takes 36 hours. Only Bhimlal and his elder son, Jitendra, earn for the family. Both work as daily-wage labourers in agriculture and allied fields with a combined monthly income of around Rs 10,000. “We are not looking for money but only justice and to empower my child to be able to live his life with dignity. We even get threat calls now and ones asking us to meet for settlement from the opposite party,” Bhimlal says. “Hamare bacche ke sath jisne galat kiya usko sajaa milni chahiye. Aisa kisi ke bacche ke sath na ho (One who wronged my child should be punished. This should not happen to any child),” he insists. For Bhimlal, every trip to court means spending money that could have gone towards household expenses, but he cannot afford to miss the hearings, he says. The family belongs to a Mahadalit community, among the most disadvantaged groups within Bihar's Scheduled Castes. The state government had in 2007 introduced the Mahadalit category to identify the most marginalised Dalit communities and direct welfare measures towards them. The family’s circumstances reflect the wider economic challenges in Kishanganj. According to NITI Aayog's 2023 report based on data from the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21), 45.55 per cent of the district's population lives in multidimensional poverty, down from 64.75 per cent in 2015-16. Its literacy rate was 57 per cent, according to the 2011 Census. The district's per capita domestic product stood at Rs 48,908 in 2023-24 (provisional), below Bihar's per capita income of Rs 69,321 in 2024-25. Train journey that changed his fate The family had been trying to bring him home even before the incident at the dairy farm. In May last year, Bhimlal and Jitendra travelled from Bihar to Kangra in Himachal Pradesh, where the boy was working. He had told them that he missed home and did not want to continue working there. The three boarded the Farakka Express train from Jind in Haryana. When it stopped at Bahadurgarh Railway Station in Jhajjar district, the boy got down to fetch water. A crowd gathered, and he could not get back on the train. His father and brother continued the journey. He was left at the station. He says a man approached him there and offered him work at a dairy farm for Rs 10,000 a month. “I believed the man as he was nice to me. He offered me water, food and work. I trusted him and agreed to go with him,” the teen recalls. He was 15 and accepted the offer thinking it would help him earn money. At the dairy farm, his day allegedly began at around 4 am and continued until 10 pm. He was made to look after cattle and do other work for 16-18 hours a day. He says he was abused and beaten for even minor mistakes. “Once I was told to carry a sack of ration for animals and I walked a bit slowly as it was heavy. The man abused me and said I was lazy. Her hurled all kinds of abuses and then gave a blow to my head with a lathi. I lost consciousness,” he recalls. The minor says he spent around two months at the farm. On July 27, 2025, while chopping fodder using a machine, he accidentally severed his left arm just above the elbow. He says the accused then cut off the remaining portion of the arm and threw it away. “I kept pleading with Anil (the main accused) for medical help but he ignored it. He tied a piece of cloth around it but the bleeding did not stop. I was begging and writhing in pain. I had to tear my T-shirt to tie it around my wound. Later, at around 8-9 pm, he put me in a vehicle only to abandon me in a forest area after two hours,” he alleges. He says he regained consciousness later and managed to get up and walk. A schoolteacher found him on July 29, 2025 – he was in Haryana by then – and informed the police. The minor was taken to a government hospital and underwent multiple surgeries. The police registered a case and began looking for the dairy farm and the accused. The farm was located on the basis of the description he provided, and the accused was arrested. Months of search, then a call For over two months, Bhimlal did not know where his son was. The family was still searching for him when the Kishanganj district administration called to say that he had been found in Haryana. Bhimlal and Jitendra travelled to see him. “After learning that he is alive, I was relieved,” says Bhimlal, “But it pained me to learn of what my child had to undergo. My elder son and I travelled to see him. His mother couldn’t stop crying. She was inconsolable throughout. Somehow, we all gathered ourselves, arranged money and travelled to get him back home.” After multiple surgeries and two months of treatment at two government hospitals, including the Post Graduate Institute of Medical Sciences (PGIMS), Rohtak, he was able to return to Kishanganj. Bhimlal hired a vehicle for Rs 20,000 to take him home by road. Given the boy's condition, he did not want to risk a train journey. The debt piled up, but he believes it was worth the expense. The teenager remembers the journey mostly for one reason – he was going to see his mother. “Raste bhar hum bas yahi sochte rahe ki kaise karke maa ke paas pahunch jayein bas. Ghar pahunche to maa se mile aur bahut rona aaya. Hum bole ki ab hum kabhi kahin nahi jayenge (All along the way, I was just thinking that I just wanted to see my mother. I reached home, met her, and cried a lot. I said I would never leave home again),” he says. Finding solace in the river, but troubles continue In Khurkhuria, the minor has once again taken up some of the things he used to do before. He wakes up between 3 am and 4 am and helps look after the family's two cows. He also helps with household work. He likes cinema and music. Swimming, however, is what he enjoys the most. The Ratwa River flows along the outskirts of the village. He goes there occasionally, sometimes to swim, at other times to just sit by the water. “Sitting beside the river, swimming in it, I have my moments of peace. I just like to be there and immerse myself in it,” he says. It remains one of the things he looks forward to when he is home. But his return has hardly meant an end to the family’s difficulties. The court case continues, and along with it, the recurring cost of travelling to Haryana. In May this year, the Haryana State Human Rights Commission ordered Rs 10 lakh compensation for the boy, observing that he had suffered physical injury and mental agony, besides sustaining a permanent disability. Bhimlal says some of the compensation has gone towards travel expenses. “I make Rs 5,000-7,000 per month but had to spend this Rs 25,000 from the compensation money because this has enabled us to keep our fight to get justice. Attending the court hearings is important. I do not want to miss any appearance in court,” he says. The family also gets recurring threats. “We have received multiple calls from different numbers threatening us and asking us to settle the matter. But I am not going to budge. I want justice for my child. This takes precedence over everything else,” Bhimlal emphasises. Advocate David Pradhan, who is representing the boy pro bono, says he too has received such calls. “They offer allurement, money, personal favours and whatnot. Now, these calls carry more threat than before. We stand firm with the family, and I have full faith in the judiciary of our country,” Pradhan says. Can the hearing be transferred? No, says Pradhan. “The jurisdiction is of Jhajjar court only. There is a provision for deposition by videoconferencing. We had initially tried applying for it, but there were some technical issues.” “Videoconferencing is available at district courts, but usually the defence counsels contest such virtual cross-examination. Cross-examination is usually preferred in person,” he adds. ‘Recounting the trauma not easy’ The trial is currently at the stage of cross-examination. Advocate Pradhan says repeatedly recounting the events has made the proceedings difficult for the teenager. “For a 16-year-old, to relive the trauma again and again takes a heavy toll on his body, mind and spirit. During his deposition on November 20, seeing his condition, the honourable court gave us a break,” he says. “I do not blame the counsel appearing for the opposite party as cross-examination is their right as per law. However, this child is going through a lot and it is really hard for him to repeatedly relive that trauma,” the counsel adds. Simultaneously, the family is also pursuing a separate process with district administrations to get a release certificate identifying the teenager as a bonded labourer. “That opens up several benefits, government schemes and benefits, including immediate cash assistance. He will also get preferential allotment of government benefits, schemes, and jobs he is qualified for,” Pradhan says. “Now, our fight is two-way. One is with the administration in different districts across three states – Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Bihar – where we are trying to prove that he was a bonded labourer. Another is in the court.” Following a report by The Indian Express in August last year, the Haryana State Human Rights Commission had taken suo motu cognisance of the case and sought a detailed medical report, a rehabilitation plan for him and an inquiry into possible violations of labour laws. In November 2025, it criticised the police probe as “incomplete, vague, and lacking in vital details.” In the wake of media reports earlier this year, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) also took suo motu cognisance of the matter. “The Commission has observed that the contents of the media report, if true, raise a serious issue of human rights violation. Therefore, it has issued notices to the Chief Secretary and the Director General of Police, Haryana as well as the Commissioner of Police, Gautam Budh Nagar, Uttar Pradesh and the District Magistrate, Kishanganj, Bihar. The response is expected from the authorities within two weeks,” a press release dated January 15 said. The NHRC also sought information on whether compensation had been paid to the boy and whether a disability certificate had been issued to enable him to access benefits under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. Long journey home and the fight ahead Now, the minor and his father are preparing for another journey – a 36-hour train ride back to Khurkhuria. He is looking forward to seeing his family. The next hearing will bring him back to Haryana, but for the moment he wants to be home. There is a lot waiting for him there: his mother, the two cows, household work, and the Ratwa River. His father, meanwhile, is thinking about the next court date and how to arrange the money to attend it. Even if he does not understand everything about the case, the teenager knows its significance. “I understand this is important. I am not ready to give up yet. Will fight this with whatever it takes,” he says.

headline: Why has BJP inducted cricketer Yuzvendra Chahal in its OBC Morcha?
content: Ahead of major elections, parties often parade celebrities who join their ranks, most of the time to contest polls. But not Yuzvendra Chahal. The Indian cricketer — who retired from first-class, red-ball cricket last year but is still available for one-day cricket and Twenty20 internationals — joined the BJP on Saturday and was appointed a special invitee to the national executive of the party’s Other Backward Classes (OBC) Morcha from Delhi, where no major election is scheduled to be held in the next few years. Chahal recently met BJP OBC Morcha’s national president and Rajya Sabha MP Amar Pal Maurya in Delhi. On Saturday, Maurya announced the new national office-bearers and members of the Morcha’s executive panel. Chahal is among the three special invitees. A BJP leader said Chahal is from the OBC Jat community and was named from Delhi because he provided the party with an address. As there are no elections around in Delhi, the party intends to invite Chahal to Morcha meetings and use him for youth outreach. In the coming Uttar Pradesh election, Jats are expected to play a crucial role in the western part of the state where they are numerically strong. In states such as UP, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Delhi, Jats are already categorised as OBC. The Jats of Rajasthan, except those in Dholpur and Bharatpur, are also OBC in the central list. They are, however, considered to be in the general category in Haryana, Chahal's home state. Jats are a politically powerful community and are estimated to influence the results of nearly 40 Lok Sabha seats and around 160 Assembly seats in UP, Haryana, Rajasthan, and Delhi. In UP, they are concentrated in the western districts, mainly cultivate sugarcane, and are the state’s richest farming community. भाजपा परिवार में मुझे स्थान व मान-सम्मान देने के लिए आदरणीय प्रधानमंत्री श्री नरेंद्र मोदी जी, आदरणीय गृहमंत्री श्री अमित शाह जी, भाजपा राष्ट्रीय अध्यक्ष श्री नितिन नवीन जी व ओबीसी मोर्चा के राष्ट्रीय अध्यक्ष श्री अमरपाल मौर्य जी का हार्दिक आभार प्रकट करता हूँ।🙏🏻 — Yuzvendra Chahal (@yuzi_chahal) November 21, 2026   “Celebrities have their own fan following and are important for optics. The party may also end up getting a new set of voters from a different age group or social group. It is good that a prominent sportsperson like Chahal, who has excelled in cricket, has joined the BJP. His presence in the party’s poll campaigns will draw the crowd of youths,” said another BJP leader. “Chahal was in touch with me and I decided to bring him in. He had shown an interest in politics and expressed a wish to work with the BJP. The induction of Chahal, Seema Samridhi Kushwaha, and Adwaita Charan Gadanayak will inspire OBC youths to connect with the BJP,” Maurya told The Indian Express. Gadanayak is a renowned sculptor from Odisha who was awarded the Padma Shri in 2025. Kushwaha, meanwhile, was the lawyer of the 2012 Delhi rape-murder victim. She had joined the BJP in March 2024 ahead of the Lok Sabha elections, and has been named to the Morcha from UP. “Yuzvendra has been inducted into the OBC team so that people know that youths from OBC communities see how successful people from the community have been on the global stage,” said a BJP leader. In a post on X on Saturday, Chahal expressed gratitude to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah, BJP national president Nitin Nabin, and Maurya for giving him “space and respect” in the party. Other cricketer-politicians Chahal is not the first cricketer to join politics. In recent years, many from the Indian cricket team have found their way into politics, including two-time World Cup winner Yusuf Pathan, who was elected to the Lok Sabha on a Trinamool Congress (TMC) ticket in 2024 and is now part of a rebel group of party MPs. Another former cricketer and TMC MP is Kirti Azad, who has sided with Mamata Banerjee. Current India men’s team coach Gautam Gambhir was the BJP MP from East Delhi from 2019 to 2024, while former India cricket captain Mohammad Azharuddin is a former Congress MP and currently a minister in Telangana. Former cricketer Navjot Singh Sidhu, an opening batsman, was a minister in the Congress-led Punjab government but has since fallen out with the party.

headline: SC directs West Bengal SIR tribunals to prioritise appeals challenging voter exclusion
content: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the appellate tribunals hearing appeals related to the West Bengal Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to give preference to pleas filed by voters challenging their exclusion from the electoral rolls, while deferring those contesting the inclusion of names.A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the tribunals to separate appeals challenging voter exclusions from those contesting inclusions, and give priority to the exclusions.Also Read: West Bengal SIR tribunals may take 12 years to decide on appeals"The second set of appeals (inclusion) does not involve any urgency, and those appeals may, for the time being, be deferred. The first set of appeals (exclusions) shall be given preference in the matter of final disposal," the bench said in its order, LiveLaw reported.The bench further directed the tribunals to prioritise, within the exclusion-related appeals, cases involving voters under the jurisdiction of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation, given that civic body elections are due to be held soon.The Supreme Court also directed the Election Commission (EC) to increase the number of appellate tribunals hearing appeals related to the West Bengal SIR, in consultation with the chief justice of the Calcutta high court.Also Read: 93% of deleted Bengal voters have won appeals, EC tells SCThe top court was hearing petitions seeking steps to streamline and expedite the disposal of appeals before the tribunals set up to address grievances arising from SIR in the state.During the hearing, advocate Prashant Bhushan, appearing on behalf of the petitioners, informed the bench that approximately 38 lakh appeals had been filed, but only around one lakh had been disposed of so far.He further submitted that over two lakh voters in the Kolkata Municipal Corporation area had allegedly been left out of the electoral rolls, with their appeals still pending.Bhushan claimed that nearly 22 lakh appeals remained unresolved and urged the bench to consider allowing the affected voters to participate in the upcoming civic body elections.Responding to the submission, Justice Bagchi observed that constituencies scheduled to go to polls could be given priority in the disposal of appeals.He also suggested increasing the number of tribunals and ensuring that they are located at more accessible places for litigants, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court.In March, the EC, acting in compliance with the Supreme Court’s directions, constituted 19 appellate tribunals to hear appeals against claims and objections rejected by judicial officers.Around 700 judicial officers from West Bengal and neighbouring states, Odisha and Jharkhand, were deployed to adjudicate approximately 60 lakh claims and objections arising from the electoral roll revision exercise.On August 25, the bench had directed the EC to submit details of pending and disposed-of appeals, with a separate count of cases filed by voters challenging their exclusion from or inclusion in the electoral rolls.The court had also asked the poll panel to specify how many additional tribunals would be needed to ensure that the appeals were decided within a stipulated timeframe.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

headline: 67% headmaster posts vacant in HP; 18% teaching posts unfilled
content: Dharamshala: Himachal Pradesh has 639 vacancies against 956 sanctioned headmaster posts, leaving nearly 67% of these positions unfilled. The shortage is also acute among computer science lecturers, with 976 of 1,786 sanctioned posts vacant, accounting for nearly 55% of the cadre.Overall, the education department has 14,754 vacant teaching posts against a sanctioned strength of 82,547, or nearly 18%, as of Nov 1, 2026, according to a reply by the education minister in the recently concluded winter session of the state Assembly.The junior basic teacher (JBT) cadre has the highest number of vacancies at 4,008 against 20,116 sanctioned posts. Another 827 of 3,264 head teacher posts and 333 of 2,098 centre head teacher posts are vacant.The department also has 1,232 vacancies among 4,464 physical education teachers (C&V) and 735 among 5,082 Shastri Sanskrit teachers. Among principals, 441 of 2,010 sanctioned posts remain vacant.Replying to a question by Congress MLA Sudhir Sharma, the education minister said the govt had no proposal to introduce a fixed recruitment calendar for batch-wise or regular teacher appointments. Recruitment, it said, depends on administrative requirements, vacancies arising from retirements and promotions, and prior approvals from the finance and personnel departments.Between Jan 2023 and Oct 2026, 5,725 teachers were appointed through different recruitment modes, including 2,375 through batch-wise recruitment. These included 1,438 JBTs, 432 TGT Arts teachers and 329 TGT non-medical teachers.Recruitment to 93 backlog physical education teacher posts remains stalled following a high court order restraining the govt from filling them on a job trainee basis. The govt also said 1,707 of 3,468 approved teacher engagements under the CBSE sub-cadre scheme remained pending.

headline: Hills teach people no one climbs very far alone, says CJI Kant
content: Dharamshala: Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant on Sunday urged students to value cooperation, patience and perseverance, saying the hills taught an essential truth that “no one climbs very far entirely alone”.Addressing the 10th convocation of the Central University of Himachal Pradesh as chief guest, he said Himachal’s villages reflected a strong community spirit, with people coming together during difficult times without any formal instruction.“If there is one lesson I hope you carry forward from the friendships and shared experiences of your university years, it is to recognise that the willingness to listen, collaborate, and learn from others is not a limitation of one’s abilities, but one of their greatest strengths,” he said.Drawing an analogy from the Dhauladhar mountains, Justice Kant said professional journeys were rarely straightforward and reaching a destination often involved winding roads, steep inclines and unexpected diversions. He advised students against comparing their progress with others.“Remember, a mountain does not become any smaller in its stature simply because another peak happens to be taller,” he said.Recalling his career, he said he began in district courts in Hisar before moving to the high court in Chandigarh, a decision that eventually became one of the most consequential choices of his professional life. “Opportunities often emerge unexpectedly, setbacks may arrive without invitation, and what initially appears to be a detour may eventually become the most important turning point of one’s journey,” he said.He also recalled his association with Himachal, where he served as high court Chief Justice before moving to Delhi, saying the warmth of its people and culture had left a lasting impression.Governor Kavinder Gupta, who presided over the convocation, urged the university to focus research on Himalayan challenges, including climate change, disaster management, water conservation and biodiversity. He said academic excellence must address society’s needs and development must remain in harmony with nature.Chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu attended the ceremony. The governor and the CJI awarded degrees and gold medals. Deputy chief minister Mukesh Agnihotri and other ministers, legislators and university officials were also present.

headline: 10th convocation of Central University of Himachal Pradesh: Achievements of daughters reflect changing India: CJI | Hindustan Times
content: Hills teach people an essential truth that no one climbs very far entirely alone, said Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant at the 10th convocation ceremony of the Central University of Himachal Pradesh in Dharamshala on Sunday. He said that a strong sense of community exists in Himachal Pradesh and can be witnessed in the villages.Along with the CJI, the convocation ceremony was also attended by Himachal Pradesh governor Kavinder Gupta and chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu.With female students bagging 21 out of 27 gold medals at the convocation, Kant said this reflects a changing India. During the convocation held on Sunday, 708 students were awarded degrees, and 27 students received gold medals. Notably, 21 of these gold medals were bagged by women students, while six were awarded to male students.Expressing his delight at this achievement, Kant said, “I am personally proud of you. The fact that women students account for such a significant majority of the gold medal recipients is not just a reflection of their individual achievements; it also speaks of a society that is steadily changing. It reflects the emergence of an India where talent is finding the opportunities it deserves, and where daughters are increasingly being provided equal opportunities to excel and move forward.”‘Don’t compare your journey with others, learn from mountains’Kant urged the graduating students to remain patient, embrace challenges and avoid comparing their achievements with others, saying that success is not always a straight-line journey and that setbacks often become important turning points in life.Addressing the convocation, Kant drew lessons from the mountains of Himachal Pradesh, saying their winding roads, steep climbs and unexpected diversions offered valuable lessons for life and professional careers.“Do not become impatient with your own progress,” he told the students, adding that professional journeys outside university would not always be straightforward and that efforts might not translate into immediate visible results. He said the distance travelled was not always apparent from where one stood.Sharing his own professional journey, the CJI recalled beginning his legal career in district courts in his native place before deciding to move to Chandigarh to practise in the high court. He said he left behind a reasonably comfortable practice and shifted with just a few pairs of clothes and considerable uncertainty about the future. In hindsight, he said, the decision proved to be one of the most consequential turning points of his career and life.‘Media should introspect on reforms it needs’Speaking to the media, Kant welcomed reforms in the judicial system, saying reforms are an essential part of the system and any further changes aimed at improving the judiciary are equally welcome. The CJI said reforms are necessary for the system to evolve and improve. “Media should have an introspection and see what reform they need,” he said.University must address Himalayan challenges through research: GuvGovernor Kavinder Gupta called upon the university to emerge as a centre of impactful research on Himalayan challenges, including climate change, disaster management, water conservation, biodiversity and rural development, stressing that universities must connect academic excellence with the needs of society.Highlighting the ecological and cultural significance of the Himalayas, the governor said development must be pursued in harmony with nature. He urged the university to promote focused research on Himalayan ecology, disaster preparedness, water resources, tribal communities, natural farming and tourism, so that academic pursuits contribute to sustainable development in the region.Education a vital foundation for devp, self-reliance: SukhuChief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu, while addressing the students, said that education is a vital foundation for development and self-reliance. He said that in an era of rapid advancements in artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology, data science, and digital technology, the education system must prepare young people not only to seek employment, but also to generate employment, undertake research, and promote innovation.The CM said that the state government considers education a vital foundation for development and self-reliance. “The government’s objective is to provide the youth of Himachal Pradesh modern knowledge and technology and enable them to establish their identity at national and international levels,” he said.He said that to promote equality in education, the state government has decided to remove the caste-related column from school admission forms from the upcoming academic session.

headline: Sukhu government pushing Himachal into debt, economic distress: Jai Ram | Hindustan Times
content: Former Himachal Pradesh chief minister and Leader of Opposition (LoP) Jai Ram Thakur on Sunday criticised CM Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu over the fiscal health of the state and alleged that all claims made by the CM, “who prides himself on being highly educated and well-read, regarding his budget-making process have proven to be hollow”.In a statement issued from Shimla, the LoP said the four budgets presented by the Sukhu government tell a story of financial mismanagement and reveal him to be a “warrior of falsehoods”. “These budgets have exposed the reality of the CM’s financial acumen, foresight, and the seriousness with which he approaches economic matters,” he said.Thakur’s statement comes at a time when Himachal’s fiscal deficit is projected to rise to ₹13,836.84 crore, which is 4.99% of the gross state domestic product (GSDP), in 2026-27, against the budget estimate of ₹9,698.03 crore (3.49% of GSDP), primarily due to the withdrawal of the revenue deficit grant (RDG) and increased revenue expenditure, according to a report tabled in the assembly during the winter session by chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu on Saturday.“For the 2026-27 fiscal year, the government had projected a fiscal deficit of ₹9,648 crore; however, within just eight months, this figure has climbed to ₹13,836 crore—an alarming increase of ₹4,188 crore, or approximately 43.4%. This occurred despite the Centre providing ₹2,529 crore more than the initial budget estimates. How has this situation arisen even after the Centre provided an additional ₹2,229 crore under centrally sponsored schemes (CSS) and an extra ₹300 crore as the state’s central share?,” said the loP.Jai Ram said that this is not merely a routine budgetary adjustment, but clear evidence of the failure of the government’s financial projections and budget planning. “Furthermore, these figures do not align with the CM’s claim of making Himachal Pradesh self-reliant by 2027. The state of the government’s fiscal discipline and management can be gauged from the fact that the supplementary budget for the year 2025-26 has reached ₹40,461 crore—amounting to 69.01% of the main budget,” he said.“When a supplementary budget becomes this large in comparison to the original budget, it naturally raises questions about the CM’s claims regarding the study and preparation undertaken before formulating the budget. Why, then, did the government fail to accurately assess the state’s revenue, expenditure, and liabilities while preparing the original budget?,” Jai Ram added.

headline: Accidents leave 4 dead in Mohali, Panchkula | Hindustan Times
content: As many as four lives were snuffed out in separate road accidents, three of them hit-and-runs, in Mohali and Panchkula districts.The first accident occurred near Tabar village on the Panchkula-Yamunanagar national highway on Sunday afternoon, claiming the life of a 63-year-old Shimla native.The deceased, identified as Rajinder Thakur, had come from Himachal Pradesh to attend a function in Raipur Rani. On Sunday, he was returning on his Honda Activa after the event when a car rammed into him.The impact was so severe that Rajinder died on the spot.On receiving information, police reached the spot and inspected the scene. The police took the car into their possession, while efforts are underway to identify its driver.Police informed the deceased’s family about the accident and initiated further proceedings in the case.In Mohali, a 22-year-old man, identified as Sarthak, died after a vehicle hit his two-wheeler in Sector 82 on Sunday. His body was sent to the Phase 6 civil hospital for autopsy.In another incident, Joginder Singh, who worked as a watchman at Ghaggar Stone Crusher in Mubarikpur, died after a tractor-trailer ran over him on November 20.His son Bhim, 53, told police that he received a phone call from the stone crusher around 7am informing him about his father’s death.According to the complaint, the tractor-trailer’s rear wheel crushed Joginder. Local reports said he was returning on foot when a tractor-trailer carrying tiles hit him. Police shifted his body to the civil hospital in Dera Bassi.Dera Bassi police registered a case on November 21 under Sections 281 and 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) against the unidentified tractor-trailer driver, who remains at large.Another scooterist was killed near Saini Majra on November 21 after a car (CH-01-BJ-3458) struck him. The victim, Hardeep Singh, was travelling from Mullanpur towards his village, Tira, when the collision occurred.The impact threw him onto the road, leaving him seriously injured. His family shifted him to Government Multi-Specialty Hospital, Sector 16, Chandigarh, where he died during treatment.The victim’s brother Kuldeep Singh lodged a complaint with the Mullanpur police, who registered a case under Sections 281, 324(4) and 106(1) of the BNS on November 21. Police are investigating all accidents and trying to trace the drivers involved.

headline: From Shraddha Kapoor To Kareena Kapoor Khan: Actresses Who Played Maharashtrian Women On Screen
content: Shraddha Kapoor will soon be seen as Tamasha and Lavani artist Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar in Eetha. She has also previously played the role of a simple Marathi girl Arohi Keshav Shirke in the blockbuster Aashiqui 2. She is half Maharashtrian and that perhaps might be the reason she does a fairly decent job at picking up the language’s nuances. Here’s Bollywood actresses who aren’t Maharashtrian but have dabbed their hands at playing Marathi mulgis on screen.Rani Mukerji - Aiyyaa (2012)Rani Mukerji is a Bengali and mostly played Punjabi, Bengali, and South Indian characters before Aiyyaa. It was in this film that the actress essayed the role of Meenakshi Deshpande, a middle-class Marathi girl whose parents are (extra) eager to get her married. However, she falls hook line and sinker for a South Indian man (Prithviraj) because of his scent and a ruckus ensues. Aiyyaa was her first time playing a Maharashtrian girl and even though she had studied Marathi in school, Rani worked on her diction and pronunciation for the role. Watch out for her dance moves in Ag bai halla machahye. Despite her doing a decent job, the film tanked.Kareena Kapoor Khan - Singham Returns (2014)The actress was born and brought up in Mumbai, so technically she can be counted as a Maharashtrian, however, she has more of a Punjabi spunk to her thanks to her paternal side of the family. When she was cast as the fiery Avni Kamat in Rohit Shetty’s Singham Returns, one wondered if she would be able to pull off the role, especially the dialect aspect of it. However, Kareena not only mouthed quite a few dialogues in chaste Marathi but spewed a few cuss words. She also wore a navari saree and showed off some cool Lavani moves in the song Mala raag yeto hai.Priyanka Chopra Jonas - Bajirao Mastani (2015)We have seen Jamshedpur born Priyanka in a Maharashtrian avatar thrice. The first was when she played Shahid Kapoor’s love interest Sweety Shekhar Bhope in Kaminey (2009). She was then cast as Kaali Gawde opposite Hrithik Roshan in Agneepath (2012). However, it was her act as Kashibai, the heartbroken wife of Bajirao (Ranveer Singh) in Bajirao Mastani that was the most impressive. Her diction, dance moves and overall look in the film was effortlessly Maharashtrian and why not, afterall she was directed by none other than Sanjay Leela Bhansali.Kangana Ranaut - Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi (2019)Born in Himachal Pradesh, Kangana dared to play the role of Rani Laxmibai in her production venture. Not only were her acting chops disappointing, she failed to get the diction and dialect of the language right. This was highlighted even more when she shared screen space with actors like Atul Kulkarni. She also played a Maharashtrian nurse Geeta Madhav Gandhare in Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata. She was slightly better here but once again couldn’t get the nuances of the language right.Kajol - Tanhaji: The Unsung Warrior (2020)Kajol is half Maharashtrian and half Bengali. The actress is seen as Savitribai Malusare, the wife of Maratha military commander Subhedar Tanhaji Malusare (Ajay Devgn), Tanhaji: The Unsung Warrior. While she didn’t prepare much for the role, she drew on family observations for her body language and in interviews spoke about how her grandmother Shobhana Samarth used to share tales of Tanhaji. In the film, even though she looked Maharashtrian, unfortunately, her diction wasn’t perfect.SPECIAL MENTION:Shilpa Shetty - Rishtey (2002)Had to mention this one. Before Vaijanti Shukla, Bollywood had seen its fair share of caricaturish fisherwomen in films. However, nothing beats the performance of Shilpa Shetty as noisy, loud and sone ke dilwali kolan. In fact, it is after her caracter enters this snoozefest, that the comatose story receives some oxygen. She showed that fisherwomen could be sexy too. Shilpa is a south Indian and yet was good in this film as far as getting the dialect, diction and look right.

headline: Band, baja, inflation: How rising prices are reshaping this wedding season
content: Naina (name changed), a lifelong Bollywood fan, always dreamed of a wedding straight out of a Karan Johar film—a grand venue, extended families in attendance, and a Manish Malhotra lehenga. But when she started planning her big day, the very first step came with a price tag that left her shocked. “Among all the wedding-related expenses, venue bookings have turned out to be the most expensive, costing much more than I had expected or budgeted for,” said the 30-year-old who is getting married this month. Naina's experience is not unique. As the wedding season begins, many families are revising their budgets as the cost of venue, food, clothes and other arrangements continues to rise. India's wedding season is expected to generate business worth ₹7.5 trillion from an estimated 5.2 million weddings between November 21 and December 15, 2026, according to the Confederation of All India Traders (CAIT). Goods and retail purchases are projected to account for ₹4.05 trillion, or 54 per cent of the estimated business, while services are expected to contribute the remaining ₹3.45 trillion. However, the celebrations are coming at a time when household budgets are already under pressure. Retail inflation rose to 6.09 per cent in October, crossing the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI's) upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent for the first time in two years. Higher food prices were a major reason for the increase. Food and venue costs push up wedding bills Food is among the biggest expenses at an Indian wedding, particularly when families host large gatherings. Rising prices of everyday ingredients are pushing up catering bills. Food retail inflation, measured by the Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI), touched a 23-month high of 8.94 per cent in October. Onions, garlic, ginger and lemons saw some of the sharpest price increases. Other ingredients used in wedding sweets and savouries, including ghee, milk, butter and curd, have also become costlier. Sanjay Kumar, a wedding venue owner in Muzaffarnagar, Uttar Pradesh, told Business Standard that higher costs of dry fruits, sugar, ghee and labour have raised per-plate catering costs in the area by nearly 25-30 per cent. Shivani Pandey (name changed), 28, who is getting married in March next year, said the per-plate cost at her chosen venue on the Gurugram-Delhi Expressway has increased from ₹3,100 at the time of booking to ₹3,575 now. “That is a considerable jump, especially when you consider the number of guests we are expecting,” Shivani said. According to IMARC’s November report, India Wedding Services Market Size, Share, Trends & Forecast (2026–2034), higher costs for venues, catering and decoration are making weddings harder to afford for lower- and middle-income families, limiting market growth despite strong demand. A Delhi-based wedding caterer told Business Standard that lower- and middle-income families are cutting guest lists and increasingly choosing venues outside Delhi and other big cities. “Venues in places such as Rishikesh and areas in Himachal Pradesh are much more affordable. For instance, a farmhouse in Delhi that would cost ₹6 lakh to book can be booked for around ₹60,000 in Rishikesh and other places outside major cities,” the caterer said. Families are also reducing spending on catering, vendors and decoration. Guest lists, traditionally a defining feature of Indian weddings, have almost halved, according to Kumar said. “Weddings that earlier had around 1,000 guests are now being scaled down to 500, while gatherings of 500 guests have shrunk to around 250,” said Kumar. Those looking to host smaller weddings are increasingly opting for dharamshalas or smaller banquet halls, he added. With gold being an important part of wedding purchases, families are looking to cut costs on other expenses, including vendors, catering and decoration. This is also reflected in venue bookings, Kumar said. "Earlier, families would book halls for two to three days to accommodate different wedding functions. Now, they are increasingly limiting bookings to just one day," he said. For some families, managing these expenses means making the difficult choice about who to leave out of the guest list. “We have decided to trim the guest list to keep the expenses under control. My father is a retired bank executive, and we have had to remove a few of his former colleagues from the guest list, as well as a few of our distant family friends. These are the kinds of adjustments we had to make to manage the rising costs,” said Shivani. Wedding wardrobe gets a rethink For many brides, the lehenga is one of the most personal parts of wedding shopping—and often one of the most expensive. Markets such as Delhi’s Chandni Chowk and Lucknow’s Aminabad draw brides looking for the right fit, designer-inspired styles and the latest social-media trends. But what is changing, shopkeepers say, is how much families are willing to spend across the wedding functions. “Wedding budgets have come down, and demand for mid-range lehengas has increased. Demand for premium lehengas has also declined,” Kamal Bhai, who owns a bridal lehenga shop in Chandni Chowk, told Business Standard. The shift comes as rising production and input costs across India's textile and ethnic wear industry push up retail prices. The impact of the West Asia war on raw material costs was felt across Surat's textile value chains, with thread, zari, embroidery and processing businesses passing on higher input costs to buyers. “Earlier, brides would buy heavy outfits for all their wedding functions, but now they are purchasing one heavy outfit for the wedding and opting for lighter ones for the other functions,” Kamal said. “The impact is mainly visible among middle- and lower-middle-income customers.” For shoppers, the price jump is not tangible. “The lehenga that I purchased back in June-July is now costing double,” said Naina. “A lehenga that earlier cost ₹30,000-40,000 is now priced at ₹70,000-80,000.” Jewellery purchases become more selective While jewellery remains one of the biggest expenses for Indian weddings, rising costs are making families more selective about the purchase. Gold prices have fluctuated sharply in 2026, rising to record highs before correcting in recent months. 24-carat gold rose from around ₹1.35 lakh per 10 grams on January 1 to a peak of ₹1.79 lakh on January 30, before falling to around ₹1.28 lakh on November 20. The 22-carat rate declined from its January peak of ₹1.64 lakh to around ₹1.17 lakh. The World Gold Council (WGC) said domestic gold prices were down 4 per cent year-to-date as of November 12, while international prices had fallen 11 per cent in US dollar terms. However, festive-season prices were nearly 10 per cent higher than a year ago, while year-on-year prices were up 17 per cent, according to its November 17 India market update. According to Om Pal Singh, who runs a jewellery store in Sector 90, Gurugram, there is not a major change in overall spending by customers during the wedding season. However, buyers are cutting down on the number of jewellery pieces they buy. "They are still purchasing essential gold jewellery, particularly pieces that they consider important for the bride to wear on her wedding day. But they are avoiding some of the additional purchases,” he said. For example, some families that prefer the bride to wear original gold jewellery are now choosing to buy only a gold necklace and earrings set, while dropping purchases such as a maang tikka, said Om Pal. “Instead, they are opting for an artificial maang tikka, which costs less," he said, adding that customers are also preferring lighter jewellery instead of heavier sets. Not everyone is feeling inflation pangs Inflation doesn't affect every wedding equally, and neither does the response to it. Neha Seth Arora, co-founder of Mumbai-based wedding planning firm Saffron String LLP, said inflation affects different segments of the market differently. "For a family working within a defined budget, the decisions can be quite practical. Do we host 500 guests or 350? Do we have an elaborate spread across every function, or make the main wedding meal the highlight?" she said. At the ultra-luxury end, Arora said the priorities can be quite different. "Families may be clear about the scale, design and level of hospitality they want to deliver, and those expectations don't necessarily change with rising costs. Instead, the focus may be on sourcing, production efficiencies and ensuring that the investment goes into the elements that have the greatest impact on the overall experience," she said. Nilanjan Banik, professor of economics and finance at Mahindra University, told Business Standard that rising inflation is likely to make India’s upcoming wedding season more expensive, but is not expected to stop large celebrations outright. "Inflation raises both the direct cost of wedding inputs and the premium charged on auspicious 'muhurat' dates. Caterers, photographers, and makeup artists may charge 1.2-1.5 times their normal rates during peak periods, while food and venue costs are estimated to rise 6-11 per cent annually," he said. Keep the vows, trim the frills Mukta Kapoor, director of Yuna Weddings & Events, said while rising costs certainly puts pressure on wedding budgets, Indian weddings are deeply personal celebrations and families are generally reluctant to compromise on what they have envisioned. "Clients are asking more questions, weighing their options and being more conscious of where their money is going. They still want a beautiful wedding, but they also want to know that what they are spending is worthwhile," said Kapoor. For Shivani, her family had to rethink a few things considering the rising costs. "But we have tried to keep the arrangements as close as possible to what we had originally planned," she said.

headline: India’s health financing and benefit incidence
content: India spent 3.29 per cent of GDP on health, or Rs 6,801 per person, according to the National Health Accounts (NHA) Estimates for India 2023-24, released in November 2026. Out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) has fallen sharply as a share of total health spending — from 64.2 per cent in 2013-14 to 42.7 per cent in 2023-24. Yet in per-capita terms it has risen, from Rs 2,767 in 2022-23 to Rs 2,901 in 2023-24. This is the paradox of Indian health policy.The state is financing a larger share of total spending, and households a smaller proportion. Absolute amounts paid by families continue to climb, however, because the disease burden is becoming more chronic, more expensive and more dependent on outpatient care.The analytical link between health outcomes and financing is shown in a research paper which I have coauthored with Kausik Bhadra and Rashmi Arora, presented at the LSE–UNU-WIDER meeting at the London School of Economics on 6 November 2026. Our method maps National Sample Survey (NSS) ailment categories to the World Health Organization’s International Classification of Diseases (ICD) and then applies benefit incidence analysis to public health spending.The evidence baseTwo complementary reports now available offer views of India’s health system that have not yet been fully integrated.The NHA 2023-24, published in November 2026 by the National Health Systems Resource Centre under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, measures who pays for health care and where the money goes, using the System of Health Accounts 2011 framework.The second is NSS Report No. 596: Household Social Consumption: Health (80th Round, January–December 2025), released by the National Statistics Office in April 2026. Covering 139,732 households, it is the eighth comprehensive all India health survey and records morbidity, hospitalisation, outpatient treatment and household medical spending. The NHA captures financing patterns of health, the NSS captures household-level experience of illness and care. Neither, however, reliably links public expenditure to internationally comparable ICD codes of morbidity. That is the missing analytical link the Chakraborty et al. method seeks to research.The International Classification of Disease (ICD) codesThe approach constructs an ICD code-based, disease-specific map of who benefits from public health spending. Concentration curves and Lorenz curves are used to test whether public spending is pro-poor or pro-rich. If the benefit concentration curve lies above the line of equality, spending is pro-poor; if it lies below the Lorenz curve, it is regressive.What the ICD mapping with Indian data showsPublic health spending is broadly pro-poor across most ICD categories. This is a significant finding that India’s public health system, whatever its weaknesses, is not being captured by elites. There is no systematic “elite capture” of public health spending.Significant gender and geographic differentials do appear. In rural areas, women often show higher benefit capture than men across several disease categories. In urban areas the pattern is more mixed, with some categories showing pro-rich utilisation among men. These inferences rest on the penultimate NSS round; the newly published 80th-round data have not yet been fully incorporated.The mapping also exposes gaps. NSS data do not cover two important WHO ICD categories — developmental anomalies and “symptoms, signs or clinical findings not elsewhere classified.” This is not a minor omission. India cannot fully account for congenital conditions, undiagnosed illness or the early stages of disease presentation.The NSS 80th RoundConducted between January and December 2025 and published in April 2026, the survey finds that 13.1 per cent of people reported illness in the preceding 15 days. Women reported higher rates than men (14.4 per cent versus 11.8 per cent). Illness rises sharply with age, 42.5 per cent of men and 45.4 per cent of women aged 60 and above reported an ailment. Urban residents reported slightly higher morbidity (14.9 per cent) than rural residents (12.2 per cent). Hospitalisation (excluding childbirth) over the preceding 365 days stood at about 2.9 per cent nationally. Men had a marginally higher rate than women (3.0 per cent versus 2.8 per cent). The gap was wider in rural areas (2.9 per cent versus 2.6 per cent). Rates peak among the elderly (around 8 per cent for those 60+) and are also elevated among young children (0–4 years).Disease-specific patternsCardiovascular disease is the leading hospitalisation category among people aged 60 and above (18.2 per cent of admissions) and a major contributor to reported illness from age 30 onwards, driven by hypertension and heart disease.Endocrine and metabolic conditions — chiefly diabetes and thyroid disorders - become significant from age 30 and require lifelong outpatient management.Infections and respiratory disease remain central in early life, infections account for 43.8 per cent of hospitalisations among children aged 0–4, while respiratory disease accounts for 13.2 per cent.Psychiatric and neurological conditions peak in young adulthood in reported illness and remain a significant share of adult hospitalisations. Injuries are especially prominent among young adults and a leading cause of hospitalisation in the 15-29 and 30-44 age groups.State-level variationInterstate differences in the Proportion of Persons Responded as Ailing (PPRA) are pronounced and deserves a deeper study using these latest data to ICD codes, applying benefit incidence analysis methodology to each state, which is beyond the scope of this article. A summary classification of major states from the recent data shows that Karnataka, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Bihar, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Chhattisgarh fall in the 10 per cent range; Odisha, Himachal Pradesh, Telangana, Punjab, Assam, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Gujarat report 11–20 per cent; West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh lie in the 21–25 per cent band; and Kerala stands out with the highest reported morbidity, exceeding 25 per cent. Kerala’s elevated PPRA is consistent with longer-standing patterns, with higher health awareness, stronger health-seeking behaviour, an older population structure and higher prevalence of chronic conditions. Lower figures in states such as Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand may reflect differences in underlying disease burden, low reporting behaviour, low access to care or demographic composition rather than strictly lower illness.Hospitalisation rates vary by age and sex across states, public facilities account for a larger share of care in rural areas, while private providers dominate more in urban settings. Institutional deliveries have become nearly universal (around 96 per cent overall). Health insurance coverage under any scheme has expanded markedly since 2017-18, reaching roughly 45-47 per cent in both rural and urban areas, driven especially by Government-sponsored schemes. Out-of-pocket medical expenditure remains substantial, particularly for private hospitalisation. These differences carry clear implications for resource allocation under the National Health Mission and state programmes, prioritising chronic disease management and elderly care in high PPRA states, while strengthening primary care, diagnostics and reporting systems in lower reporting states. Age and gender gradients, higher burden on females and the elderly, appear broadly consistent across regions.The financing mismatchGovernment health expenditure has tripled in nominal terms, from Rs 1.30 lakh crore in 2013-14 to Rs 4.14 lakh crore in 2023-24. Per capita Government health spending rose from Rs 1,042 to Rs 2,959 over the same period. Yet the share of Government spending in GDP remains low, total health expenditure in 2023-24 was 3.29 per cent of GDP, with Government spending at only 1.43 per cent, still well below the 3-4 per cent threshold widely regarded as necessary for meaningful progress toward universal health coverage.India has increased public spending, but not enough to offset the growing burden of chronic disease. The result is a system in which households (oope) continue to pay a large and rising absolute amount even as their share of total spending falls. The household budgets go catastrophic, with rising burden of health spending.The policy imperativeThe evidence points to a clear priority. India must raise Government health spending toward at least 3 per cent of GDP while simultaneously improving the targeting and efficiency of that spending. The ICD-based benefit incidence framework in my coauthored paper offers a practical instrument. It allows policymakers to see which diseases consume public resources, which populations benefit, and where gaps remain. It also supports geographical and sex-disaggregated analysis, essential given the gender patterns revealed by the NSS. The 80th-round NSS supplies the morbidity map. The NHA supplies the financing map. The ICD-based benefit incidence method supplies the analytical link between resources and outcomes.What India now needs is to use that benefit incidence analysis framework systematically to build a health system that is both financially protective and epidemiologically responsive.The writer is professor at NIPFP, Ministry of Finance, Govt of India and also research affiliate at the Levy Economics Institute of Bard College, New York; Views presented are personal.
