headline: Himachal to Recruit Temporary Teachers in Technical Institutions Through State Chayan Commission
content:
The Himachal Pradesh government has notified the Engagement Policy-2026 to streamline the recruitment of temporary teachers in government technical educational institutions and address the shortage of teaching staff across the state.

Under the new policy, recruitment for temporary teaching positions in Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs), polytechnics, engineering colleges and pharmacy institutions will be conducted through the Himachal Pradesh State Chayan Ayog on the basis of an open competitive examination.

According to the notification issued by the Department of Technical Education, Vocational and Industrial Training, appointments will be made, as per institutional requirements, to the posts of Assistant Craft Instructor, Assistant Lecturer and Junior Professor. The existing reservation roster will be followed during recruitment, although no new regular posts will be created under the policy.

The selected candidates will initially be engaged for a period of one year. Their tenure may be extended annually by the Director of Technical Education, depending on institutional requirements and individual performance. However, the maximum engagement period will be five years, after which their services will automatically come to an end.

The policy makes it clear that these appointments will be purely temporary and non-cadre in nature. The selected candidates will not have any right to claim regularisation or permanent adjustment in government service. Instead of regular pay scales and allowances, they will be paid a fixed monthly honorarium.

The minimum age for applicants has been fixed at 21 years and the maximum at 45 years. Age relaxation will be provided to candidates belonging to reserved categories in accordance with existing government rules.

headline: Himachal Pradesh plans four new townships across Shimla, Solan, Sirmaur and Kangra
content:
The Gulf conflict has disrupted global supply chains, pushed...

REITs have changed the way commercial real estate is owned a...

What really powers the cloud? Behind every Google search, A...

Luxury real estate is one of the most talked-about segments ...

Himachal Pradesh is planning four new townships at Jathia Devi in Shimla, Sheetalpur in Solan, Surla Janot in Sirmaur and Lanj in Kangra, according to a written reply in the state Assembly. The Jathia Devi project proposes 157 residential plots and 762 apartments, alongside commercial and community facilities. Land has been transferred for the proposed Him Chandigarh township at Sheetalpur, while government land has been identified at Surla Janot. Land selection is continuing at Lanj. No construction timelines or additional budget allocations have been announced.

Himachal Pradesh is planning to develop four new townships at Jathia Devi in Shimla, Sheetalpur in Solan, Surla Janot in Sirmaur and Lanj in Kangra, according to information placed before the state Assembly in response to a written question by BJP MLA Sudhir Sharma, who represents the Dharamshala constituency. The proposed developments are at different stages of planning and land identification, with Jathia Devi having progressed further in terms of its project approvals and proposed residential facilities. The government said no final construction timeline had been fixed for any of the four townships. Jathia Devi, located on the outskirts of Shimla, is planned to have 157 residential plots, including spaces for bungalows and villas, and 762 apartments with one-, two- and three-bedroom configurations. The proposed development also includes six commercial retail units, two mixed-use plots, a school and a community building. The project has received approval from the Town and Country Planning Department, while an application for registration with the Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA) has been submitted. The second proposed development, Him Chandigarh, is planned at Sheetalpur in the Baddi area of Solan district. The government informed the Assembly that 7,042 bighas and 18 biswas of government land earmarked for the township had been transferred to the Housing Department. The process to acquire a further 8,435 bighas and four biswas of private land has also commenced. A notification for a social impact assessment has been issued as part of the acquisition process. In Sirmaur district, 133 bighas of government land have been identified for the proposed township at Surla Janot. The project is still at the land identification and transfer stage, and the government has not specified its proposed residential capacity. The fourth location is Lanj in Kangra district, where the process of identifying suitable land is still underway. The number of residential plots, flats or villas proposed at Sheetalpur, Surla Janot and Lanj has not yet been determined, according to the information reported. The government also clarified that no separate policy specifically governing the development of these new townships had been notified. No additional budget had been allocated for the four projects at the time of the Assembly reply. The statement did not provide details of the overall estimated investment, funding arrangements or infrastructure development plans for the proposed townships. The four projects therefore remain at different stages, ranging from planning and departmental approval at Jathia Devi to land transfer, acquisition and identification at the other locations. The government has not announced a common implementation schedule for the developments.

headline: How to secure your WhatsApp Web sessions against fraud
content: The National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU) of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that authenticated WhatsApp Web sessions could, under certain circumstances, be misused to gain unauthorised access to users’ WhatsApp accounts.An advisory issued by the I4C, the cyber security arm of the Union Home Ministry, said such unauthorised access could allow malicious persons to read messages, send messages while impersonating users, access contacts and group conversations, and misuse the account holder's trusted identity for fraud, phishing, social engineering and other malicious activities.Users have been advised to exercise caution while using WhatsApp Web, particularly on office computers, shared systems, public computers or devices accessible to others.Listing a series of precautionary measures, the I4C advised users to avoid exchanging official or sensitive information through WhatsApp Web."Government, organisational, financial, confidential or other sensitive information should preferably not be exchanged through WhatsApp Web sessions on computers," the advisory said.It also cautioned users against keeping WhatsApp Web permanently logged in and advised them to avoid leaving authenticated sessions active when not required, particularly on office or shared computers.The advisory stressed the importance of logging out after every session, warning that simply closing the browser window or tab should not be treated as logging out."Develop a habit of manually logging out from WhatsApp Web after completing your work," it said.If using WhatsApp Web is unavoidable, the I4C suggested opting for Incognito or Private Browsing mode on a trusted computer and manually logging out before closing the browser.The advisory also cautioned users against logging in from cyber cafes, public kiosks, hotel business centres, borrowed computers or other untrusted systems.Users have further been advised to remain alert to unusual account activity. Unexpected messages sent from their accounts, unusual replies from contacts or unexplained activity should be treated seriously.The I4C also recommended keeping operating systems, browsers and security software updated and avoiding suspicious downloads, unknown files, cracked software and untrusted applications.

headline: 'Unable to digest': BJP takes jibe at Rahul Gandhi after India ranks 3rd on Asia Power Index
content: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Monday attacked the Congress and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, saying that they were unable to acknowledge the country's achievements on the global stage after the Asia Power Index report named India as Asia's third most powerful country, only behind the US and China.Australian think tank Lowy Institute released its Asia Power Index Ranking for 2026, where India retained its "major power" status in Asia and increased its overall score to 40.5, despite a dip in economic capability. The report also noted that India stood strong in the diplomatic field, making Prime Minister Narendra Modi Asia's second-most effective leader behind Xi Jinping.The BJP lauded the report, calling it a testament to India’s growing strategic, economic, diplomatic and cultural power along with PM Modi's effective leadership.Also Read | Rahul Gandhi says BJP, RSS have ‘no understanding’ of India's spiritual traditions'Rahul Gandhi unable to digest India's achievements'Taking to X, BJP leader Sambit Patra said the report reflected India's progress in diplomatic influence, future resources, economic relationships, and defence networks, adding that the country was establishing its identity as a global power.Attacking Rahul Gandhi and the Congress, Patra said, “While the world is acknowledging India’s growing strength and global leadership, Rahul Gandhi and the Congress party are constantly trying to spread negativity by questioning the country’s achievements.” "Rahul Gandhi should explain why the Congress party has trouble acknowledging the country’s achievements when international institutions are recognising India’s growing power and the effective leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi," he added.While addressing a rally in Telangana, BJP national president Nitin Nabin also attacked Rahul Gandhi over the latter's remarks on the Indian economy, saying the country was advancing significantly even by global standards. Nabin remarked that India was counted among the "fragile five" during the Congress-led UPA regime, but emerged as the world's fourth-largest economy under the leadership of Prime Minister Modi.Union Minister Kiren Rijiju said India has risen and moved far ahead under the leadership of PM Modi. "If the opposition doesn't praise us, it doesn't mean they are right. They have their right to speak, but the country has changed. India has moved far ahead," he was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.BJP MP Ravi Shankar Prasad accused Gandhi of spreading falsehoods about India on foreign soil and ignoring the country's achievements on the global stage. "Prime Minister Modi is the second most influential leader in Asia among regional leaders today, after Xi Jinping. India is the only country whose economic ties with other countries have not declined," he said at a press briefing.Congress reacts to Lowy Institute's reportCongress MP Manish Tewari acknowledged the findings of the Asia Power Index report, saying India had always been a major power and did not need endorsement from other parties."Lowy Institute is a respected think tank in Australia," he told IANS. “India has had its own standing in the world going back to 1947. We have always been a major power. We do not really need anybody's endorsement to know our intrinsic strengths. Suffice to say that think tanks keep coming out with reports from time to time. Lowy Institute is a respected institute, and I will definitely peruse that report.” What did the report say?While the US and China continued to dominate Asia's power rankings, the report showed that the power gap between the two largest economies had narrowed to its lowest levels since 2018. This gap comes due to US President Donald Trump's conflict with Iran in the West Asia region, which has diverted Washington's attention and resources from the continent.Meanwhile, India remained an influential force in Asia due to its regional trade and investment ties, despite a dip in its economic potential due to a weakening rupee and a drop in outbound investment.

headline: Mind the Gap: Insurance can cushion losses from floods, cyclones and other disasters
content: Act of God perils, also known as natural catastrophe risks, are among the most common and unpredictable threats faced by individuals, businesses and communities. They can damage a wide range of assets, including residential and commercial properties, household contents, business equipment, machinery, electronic devices and motor vehicles. Almost any physical asset located in an affected area is vulnerable to loss or damage. These perils include naturally occurring events such as earthquakes, floods, storms, cyclones, tsunamis, landslides, cloudbursts, droughts and other extreme weather or geological events. They are not caused by human intervention and cannot be prevented or avoided. As climate patterns become increasingly volatile, their economic and social impact has grown, compounded by insurance gaps. The scale of the challenge is evident from the Sixteenth Finance Commission Report, which examined five major disaster events: Kerala floods and heavy rainfall (2018-19), Cyclone Amphan in Bengal (2020-21), prolonged drought in Rajasthan (2021-22), Cyclone Michaung and associated floods in Tamil Nadu (2023-24), and floods, cloudbursts and landslides in Himachal Pradesh (2023-24). Economic losses across these events exceeded ₹99,000 crore, with more than 90 per cent remaining uninsured. Indirect losses, including income disruption and prolonged recovery, were estimated at 1.5 to 2.5 times the direct physical damage. These findings underline the financial protection gap and the role of insurance in helping individuals, businesses and communities finance recovery. (Source: Sixteenth Finance Commission) Property insurance: Provides financial protection against physical loss or damage to insured property from covered risks, including specified Act of God perils such as earthquakes, STFI (storm, tempest, flood and inundation) and landslides. Coverage can extend to homes, apartments, offices, shops, malls, warehouses, hotels, schools, hospitals and other commercial or institutional properties. It may also cover contents such as furniture, fixtures and fittings, electrical installations, office equipment and stock, subject to policy terms.

headline: Avoid WhatsApp Web for sensitive, official work: Ministry of home affairs flags cybersecurity risks | India News
content: The National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU) of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that authenticated WhatsApp Web sessions could be misused to gain unauthorised access to users’ accounts, allowing malicious actors to read messages, impersonate account holders and access their contacts and group conversations.In an advisory released on Monday, home affairs ministry's I4C warned WhatsApp users that authenticated WhatsApp Web sessions could be misused to gain unauthorised access to their accounts, allowing malicious actors to read private messages, impersonate users and exploit their identities for fraud, phishing and other cybercrimes.The advisory recommended avoiding use of WhatsApp Web for official and sensitive environments.The agency has advised users to exercise caution, particularly while accessing WhatsApp Web on office computers, shared systems or public devices. “Users are therefore advised to exercise caution while using WhatsApp Web, particularly on office computers, shared systems, public computers or devices that may be accessible to other persons,” the advisory said, as it listed out precautionary measures to use WhatsApp web safely and without getting trapped in a cybercrime.The government advised users to avoid official, sensitive work on WhatsApp Web. “Government, organizational, financial, confidential or other sensitive information should preferably not be exchanged through WhatsApp Web session on computers,” it said.It also asked users to not keep WhatsApp Web permanently logged in. “Avoid leaving an authenticated WhatsApp Web session active when it is not required, particularly on office or shared computers,” it said.The advisory further added that users should make it a point to log out manually after each session as simply closing the browser window or tab should not be treated as logging out.Use Incognito/Private Browsing mode when use is unavoidable. If WhatsApp Web must be used temporarily, use Incognito/Private Browsing mode on a trusted computer and manually log out before closing the browser, it said.Users have also been warned against using WhatsApp Web from unknown or public computers at cyber cafes, public kiosks, hotel business centres, borrowed computers or other untrusted systems.“Be alert to unusual account activity. Unexpected messages sent from your account, unusual replies from contacts or unexplained activity should be treated seriously,” it said.The I4C has advised users to keep devices, operating systems and browsers secure, the security software updated and avoid suspicious downloads, unknown files and cracked software.

headline: Utilise AI Technology To Achieve Better Outcomes In Public Services: CM
content: Amaravati: Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu directed officials to leverage Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology across various sectors, from health care to agriculture, to achieve better outcomes. He called for the effective use of modern technology and AI Stack to simplify government services, improve the performance of departments and enhance government revenues.During a review of Real Time Governance (RTGS), the Chief Minister instructed officials to take measures to ensure faster and more efficient delivery of citizen services provided by government departments. He also stressed the need to organise capacity-building programmes to enhance the skills and capabilities of government employees.The Chief Minister observed that a positive public perception of government services would create greater opportunities to deliver better governance. He directed officials to ensure speedy resolution of public grievances received through the Public Grievance Redressal System (PGRS). He called upon senior officials to address gaps in monitoring public grievance redressal and ensure that every department continuously reviews its performance.Emphasising the growing importance of data-driven decision-making, he said that it would play a crucial role in governance in the future. The Chief Minister noted that the recently held local body elections served as an indicator of the government's performance. He directed senior officials of all departments to further strengthen monitoring mechanisms and work towards delivering better and more efficient services to the people.

headline: PM Modi’s Principal Secretary P K Mishra on ‘decisive leadership’: What are lessons in ethics?
content: (UPSC Ethics Simplified, a special series under UPSC Essentials by The Indian Express, examines ethical dilemmas through contemporary issues. This edition draws on the idea of decisive leadership to explore moral responsibility, public service values and citizen-centric governance.) Let's begin with a question: A senior government official must decide whether to implement a policy that can deliver immediate benefits to a large section of the population but may create difficulties for a smaller, vulnerable group. The decision is urgent, and delaying it could affect public welfare. What should guide the official's decision? A. Choose the option that benefits the largest number, even if some citizens face unfair consequences. B. Delay the decision until every stakeholder agrees with the proposed course of action. C. Take a timely, evidence-based decision after considering its impact on different groups, while ensuring fairness and accountability. D. Follow the established procedure without considering the specific circumstances of affected citizens. At the inaugural national workshop on ‘Leadership as Mission’, organised by NITI Aayog on November 17, Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister P K Mishra highlighted how India's governance journey has been shaped by decisive leadership and the ability to translate vision into action. Citing examples ranging from the response to the 2001 Kutch earthquake and the COVID-19 pandemic to India's expanding presence in the global space economy and the Lakhpati Didi initiative, he underlined how political will, responsive administration and mission-driven governance can bring meaningful change to people's lives. The workshop is part of a series of five national workshops aimed at documenting leadership experiences and developing case studies and learning material for civil services training institutions, educational institutions and universities. But what makes leadership truly decisive? Is it merely the ability to take quick decisions, or does it also involve ensuring that those decisions improve citizens' lives? What is decisive leadership? Understanding its relationship with citizen experience Do you remember why Mahatma Gandhi chose to visit people affected by communal tensions when the rest of India was celebrating Independence? On his way to Noakhali, he arrived in Calcutta on August 9, 1947, and stayed to quell communal unrest. He observed Independence Day on August 15 through fasting, prayer and spinning khadi. His decision to remain in Calcutta was a moral choice. He was prepared to take upon himself the suffering of citizens. It reflected leadership rooted in moral conviction and a commitment to public welfare. Decisive leadership and citizen experience are complementary concepts. Without ethical foundations, decision-making can lack the wisdom needed to ensure positive outcomes for citizens. Ethical leadership means guiding decisions through moral principles such as integrity, fairness and public interest. It transforms decision-making from arbitrary or self-serving action into fair, citizen-centric governance. When guided by morality, decisive leadership involves taking clear, evidence-based decisions in a timely manner and accepting responsibility for their outcomes. Citizen experience refers to the quality of people's overall interactions with government services and institutions. It includes accessibility, fairness, respect, responsiveness and trust. These principles connect leadership with citizens' everyday experiences. Without them, even swift decisions can result in unfair, opaque or harmful outcomes, undermining the legitimacy of institutions. Ethical foundations of decisive leadership: Moral responsibility and public service values Decisive leadership improves citizen experience through speed and clarity. Without timely decisions and clarity of thought, governance cannot be effective, and the delivery of benefits may remain inadequate. Not taking a decision is itself a decision. Since Independence, citizens have often faced delays in their interactions with the executive, ambiguity in procedures and repeated visits to access government services. Addressing these obstacles requires an ethical leadership mindset. Leaders who set priorities, simplify processes and make timely, sometimes real-time, decisions can improve service delivery. Recent public discourse also indicates that citizens want to be heard, receive prompt decisions and be treated with respect. This makes three values particularly important: Responsiveness: The ability and willingness of public institutions to address citizens' needs promptly. Accountability: The obligation of public officials to explain their decisions and accept responsibility for their actions. Empathy: Understanding and considering another person's circumstances and perspective. How does decisive leadership improve citizen experience? To create a better citizen experience, leaders must ensure consistency in their behaviour and actions. Consistency means applying principles and decisions reliably over time. It builds trust, which is the confidence citizens place in the government's capabilities and intentions. The early and robust interventions seen in some instances during the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated how decisive action, when combined with effective communication and evidence-based decision-making, can improve outcomes and strengthen public support. Research on the public sector suggests that effective leaders possess strong character, a clear purpose or vision, and the ability to deliver results even with limited resources. Prioritising citizen satisfaction has consistently emerged as an important operational approach. Other qualities that contribute to a better citizen experience include: Reliability: Being dependable and consistently fulfilling commitments. Empathy: Listening to and respecting others while understanding their concerns. High aspirations: Setting ambitious goals to improve public outcomes. Continuous learning: Being open to feedback, new knowledge and improving existing practices. Trust, empathy and accountability: Building citizen-centric institutions Well-defined roles, goals and monitoring mechanisms provide clarity in administration. This, combined with attention to interpersonal dynamics through support and empowerment, improves the quality of frontline services. Empowerment means giving individuals the authority, resources and confidence to perform their responsibilities effectively. When frontline officials are supported and empowered, citizens are more likely to experience an administration that is sensitive to their needs and worthy of their trust. In ethical governance, it is important to break the slumber and listen more to people at large. Listening and responding to people's concerns are key aspects of decisive leadership (The writer is the author of ‘Being Good’, ‘Aaiye, Insaan Banaen’, ‘Kyon’ and ‘Ethikos: Stories Searching Happiness’. He teaches courses on and offers training in ethics, values and behaviour. He has been the expert/consultant to SAARC countries, UPSC, Central Bureau of Investigation( CBI),National Judicial Academy, ATI, RAKNPA, Haryana Institute of Public Administration, ISA MountAbu, National Centre for Good Governance,Competition Commission of India (CCI), etc. He has PhD in two disciplines and has been a Doctoral Fellow in Gandhian Studies from ICSSR. His second PhD is from IIT Delhi on Ethical Decision Making among Indian Bureaucrats. He writes for the UPSC Ethics Simplified (concepts and caselets) weekly.) headline: US banks tighten AI agent controls after OpenAI and Hugging Face incidents raise security concerns | Hindustan Times
content: Several large and mid-sized US banks are tightening controls around their own artificial intelligence agents to prevent them from going rogue, after high-profile incidents at ​technology firms exposed potential weaknesses, banking and industry sources said.US banks had already been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions while also cracking down on how ‌their own internally-developed agents function. The move to scrutinize internal agents is a reaction to experimental OpenAI models escaping testing safeguards and gaining access to systems at the ChatGPT maker, Hugging Face and other organizations, after which several banks set up internal teams to examine their systems.To avoid incidents such as those at Hugging Face, a number of US banks are now limiting what internal agents within their own bank can access, for example by separating them from critical systems and improving their ability ​to spot and stop harmful activity, four sources familiar with the matter said.The banks are limiting how long agents can keep working, keeping passwords and records beyond their reach, and creating backup plans to keep ​operations running if an agent has to be shut down, one of the sources said.They are also more firmly separating agents from other technology, tightening ⁠restrictions on what they can access and bringing them within existing identity and access-management programs, two of the sources said. In addition, they are restricting the credentials given to agents, limiting the activities and systems they ​are authorized to access, and keeping testing environments isolated from systems used in day-to-day banking operations, according to two of the sources.The Hugging Face incident - when an OpenAI model went rogue and triggered a hack that ​compromised the AI startup's infrastructure - had a chilling effect on banks' adoption of the latest AI models, one source said, prompting tighter limits on the credentials, activities and systems available to internal agents.And while no banks have been so far affected in such incidents, several large and mid-sized banks assembled internal teams to study how the models bypassed restrictions, assess whether similar weaknesses existed in their own systems and recommend additional protections, the sources said.Also read: AI data centres drive US construction jobs as skilled trades offer new career paths beyond collegeAll the major US banks deploy agentic AI ​across businesses including wealth management, payments, transactions and other corporate functions. Unlike conventional software, agents can independently make decisions, use tools and interact with multiple systems to complete a task.The banks already face challenges from having to rapidly update ​and fix newly discovered vulnerabilities, as easily accessible AI tools and large language models supercharge the discovery of vulnerabilities in software. JPMorgan earlier this week was hit with a software bug.KILL SWITCHESAs part of the tighter controls, banks are treating ‌agents more ⁠like employees, with clearly defined credentials, permissions and limits, one of the sources said. Institutions also need to record which systems an agent accessed, what actions it took and whether a person approved them, the person said.Banks are more firmly separating passwords, activity records and critical security controls from AI agents, reinforcing existing safeguards intended to prevent agents from altering evidence of their actions. While some of these access controls already existed, banks have since then tested, reinforced or extended them as needed, three of the sources said.Such records allow investigators to reconstruct an incident and determine what data or systems were affected, one of the sources said.Banks ​are also studying how to detect when an agent ​starts using credentials assigned to a human ⁠employee and are reviewing "kill switches" to disconnect malfunctioning or compromised agents from other systems and identify any processes they created, four sources said.Because shutting down an agent can disrupt operations, banks are testing backup processes for functions such as loan processing, fraud detection and financial-crime reviews, one of the sources said.Banks are now ​also limiting how much work an agent can do, reducing the cost and potential damage if it goes wrong, one of the sources said."Banks are ​putting much greater emphasis on ⁠post-deployment monitoring and risk management for AI agents," said Naresh Raheja, an independent AI risk management specialist and former Office of the Comptroller of the Currency official. "Unlike traditional models, agents can exhibit behaviors after deployment that were not identified during testing and validation."BYPASSING CONTROLSThe tighter controls were prompted by the OpenAI and Hugging Face incidents. During cybersecurity tests in July, the OpenAI models bypassed controls intended to isolate them from the internet and exploited software vulnerabilities to access ⁠external systems. ​OpenAI said the models had been tested with fewer safeguards than those used in its public products.The episode showed that written ​instructions alone may not prevent an AI agent from taking unwanted actions, one of the sources said.Some banks have separately warned about the risks of unauthorized external agents accessing customer accounts."We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside ​the company because that's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan said during the bank's third-quarter earnings call.

headline: Trisha Fans Launch Ilayapuratchi Thalaivi Trisha Peravai
content: A fan organisation in Tamil Nadu, linked to actor Trisha, has launched a welfare forum called Ilayapuratchi Thalaivi Trisha Peravai, likening her to former Chief Minister J Jayalalithaa. The group, established under the leadership of Tirunelveli Rajagopal, has dubbed Trisha as Jayalalithaa Junior, citing similarities in governance style and suggesting she may enter politics. While the fans' organisation seems to project a political career for the actor, Trisha has not made any official statements regarding political ambitions so far.

headline: Jharkhand’s legacy must not be separated from Birsa Munda’s vision
content: The Jharkhand government observed Birsa Munda’s birth anniversary on November 15. However, the usual celebration of Jharkhand’s formation day on November 15 was extended to November 28, given the coincidence with Chhath Puja. The decision to postpone the celebration is likely an administrative decision and not a political statement. While Chhath is equally significant and the government’s decision to observe the festival is fair, overlooking the historical significance of November 15 could mean overlooking the reason why Jharkhand holds its political identity today. The commemoration of Birsa Munda’s birth anniversary cannot be separated from the celebrations of Jharkhand’s formation. The two historical occasions, in their entirety, share the history of Adivasi assertion. The larger aspiration of Birsa Munda’s Ulgulan was that Adivasi communities should exercise control over their land, resources, institutions, and ways of life. His rebellion was rooted in the assertion of Abua Disom, Abua Raj — our land, our rule. He emerged as a leader who brought people together to fight against not only the British oppression of the Adivasi communities, but also to resist the dispossession of Adivasis from their land, the exploitative zamindari system, and to resist the erosion of self-governance. The creation of Jharkhand on November 15, 2000, was not happenstance; it deliberately coincided with the birth anniversary of Birsa. The state’s foundation day, then, became a political statement of the historical demands of Adivasis and their self-rule. It was more than just an administrative unit carved out of Bihar — it was an acknowledgement that Adivasis have the right to decide their future. The movement was significant in its ability to put Adivasis and their needs at the centre. However, the community continues to struggle in the economic, social, political, and administrative spheres. After 26 years of recognised statehood, the question is still frequently asked: Has the separate institutional recognition of a tribal state fulfilled the promise of self-rule? Has the promise translated into control over the pillars of self-determination? The gap between statehood and self-rule that arises from these questions can be seen in the state’s relationship with its geography, resources, and language. The Chota Nagpur Tenancy (CNT) Act and Santhal Parganas Tenancy (Supplementary Provisions) Act were enacted to protect Adivasi land rights and self-governance. Yet mining projects, legal loopholes, and weak enforcement continue to fuel conflicts and land alienation across Jharkhand. These gaps in self-rule have gradually extended to language and knowledge. Jharkhand has institutionalised programmes like PALASH and has come up with a separate department for tribal languages in universities. But one often wonders whether the Adivasi languages are ingrained in the state’s institutional routine — in educational institutions, public administration and policymaking — or are they merely confined to symbolic celebration? Jharkhand, as a whole, remains an understudied and neglected state. And the idea of “Abua Sarkar”, as things stand, must not only focus on the recognition of Adivasi identity and history, but should forge ahead with self-rule and collective liberation. The concept of Abua Sarkar — our government — is a political promise, a political security. A political space where the government reconsiders who controls the land, which languages go around the corridors in state-led institutions, whose knowledge systems supervise the leadership, and whose voices are paramount in decision-making. Birsa’s legacy transcends history. To engage with what he stood for is to question the experience of Adivasis in contemporary Jharkhand. A separate state was a demand for an agency, which would work based on the political and administrative framework that Dharti Aaba built. And while public commitments may explain this deferral of the date to celebrate this agency, for the Adivasis, who have forever stayed at the margins of the mainstream narratives, this is history moved in the calendar. For those whose histories have been sidelined, the commemoration of Jharkhand’s formation is not just an official statehood celebration; it is for collective remembrance and reaffirmation of identity. The date matters. It is, after all, a socio-historical anchor that contextualises and fosters a sense of a rebellion that continues. Jharkhand’s foundation, in all its glory, derives its distinctive meaning from Birsa’s Ulgulan. The writer is sub-editor, The Indian Express. shriya.murmu@expressindia.com

headline: How Indian companies can successfully implement Artificial Intelligence
content: India stands at a decisive point in its technological journey. With nearly 1.5 million engineering graduates each year, over 2.23 lakh recognised start-ups, and a payments network that processed 24.51 billion UPI transactions in a single month, the country is well placed to benefit from artificial intelligence. However, many Indian enterprises have launched pilots that never reached production. In an EY–CII survey of over 200 enterprise leaders, 47% reported multiple generative AI use cases in production, yet more than half reported pilot-to-production success rates below 10%. Successful adoption is less a technological challenge than an organisational one, as a 2024 study by BCG found that about 70% of implementation challenges arise from people and processes, 20% from technology, and 10% from algorithms.Is the main problem business or technology?The most common cause of failure in AI programmes is the pursuit of technology for its own sake. Leadership teams, influenced by global enthusiasm, sometimes mandate that the organisation ‘adopt AI’ without defining what it should achieve, producing disconnected experiments with no clear owner or return. Globally, 74% of companies surveyed by BCG had yet to show tangible value from AI.A more disciplined approach starts with the business. Leaders should identify the processes where cost, delay, error, or missed opportunity is greatest, then assess whether AI is the appropriate remedy. A bank may target underwriting and fraud detection; a manufacturer, predictive maintenance; a retailer, demand forecasting. Each use case should be tied to a specific metric, such as turnaround time, cost per transaction, or defect rate. BCG’s AI leaders pursued about half as many opportunities as their peers and expected more than twice the return. McKinsey found that, of 25 organisational attributes tested, redesigning workflows had the greatest effect on bottom-line impact from generative AI, yet only 21% of firms had fundamentally redesigned any workflow.Build strong data foundationsAI systems are only as reliable as their data. Many Indian organisations, particularly long-established firms, hold information in fragmented legacy systems and departmental silos. Gartner predicts that through 2026 organisations will abandon 60% of AI projects not supported by AI-ready data, and found that 63% of surveyed organisations lacked confidence in their data management practices for AI. Companies should therefore invest in data engineering before, or alongside, model development: consolidating sources, establishing common definitions, improving quality, and setting clear ownership and access protocols. Although less glamorous than deploying a sophisticated model, this work is frequently the greatest determinant of success, and EY–CII respondents cited data readiness, integration, and governance as persistent bottlenecks.Develop talent and leadership capabilityExperienced professionals in machine learning, data engineering, and AI product management remain scarce; Nasscom estimates that India could face a shortfall of more than 600,000 AI professionals by 2027. A balanced strategy therefore combines targeted recruitment with extensive upskilling. Leadership understanding is equally important. McKinsey found that CEO oversight of AI governance was the element most correlated with bottom-line impact from generative AI, yet only 28% of AI-using organisations reported it. Executives need not become technical experts, but they must grasp what AI can and cannot do and allocate resources realistically. Appointing an accountable executive and forming cross-functional teams of domain experts, data scientists, and engineers tends to work better than confining AI to an isolated technology department. A model built without input from the people who understand the process is unlikely to be adopted.Choose the right approach: Build, buy, or partnerNot every company should develop its own models. In MIT’s NANDA study, tools purchased from specialised vendors or built in partnership succeeded about 67% of the time, against roughly one-third for internal build. The study rests on interviews, a survey, and an analysis of public deployments, so the figures are indicative. Building in-house is justified where the capability offers genuine competitive differentiation or involves highly sensitive proprietary data. For routine applications such as document processing, customer service automation, or internal knowledge search, buying or configuring existing tools is the more prudent course.Partnerships with start-ups, academic institutions, and technology providers can supplement internal capacity. The IndiaAI Mission, approved in 2024 with an outlay of ₹10,372 crore, has onboarded more than 38,000 GPUs offered to Indian start-ups and academia at affordable rates, which may reduce barriers for smaller enterprises.Addressing problems in the Indian contextAI solutions designed for Western markets often require adaptation for India. Customers communicate in dozens of languages and frequently mix them within a single conversation, yet benchmark tests show leading models perform significantly worse in Indic languages than in English. Companies serving a broad domestic audience should favour systems that handle Indian languages, and may benefit from public efforts such as Bhashini, which supports more than 22 languages.Cost sensitivity is another consideration. Indian markets reward affordable solutions, which encourages appropriately sized models and careful monitoring of computing expenses; the cost of GPT-3.5-level inference fell more than 280-fold between late 2022 and late 2024. Uneven connectivity outside major cities may also influence design, particularly for field operations, agriculture, and rural financial services. India’s experience with digital public infrastructure, such as Aadhaar and UPI, shows that solutions built for scale and inclusion can succeed when designed around local conditions.Establishing governance, ethics, and complianceResponsible deployment is both an ethical duty and a commercial necessity. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 imposes obligations on how organisations collect, process, and safeguard personal data. DPDPA’s rules were notified in November 2025, with most operative duties, including consent, security safeguards, and breach notification, applying from May 2027. Systems should therefore be designed for compliance now rather than retrofitted. India has chosen not to enact a standalone AI law: MeitY’s November 2025 AI Governance Guidelines are voluntary and principle-based, relying on existing legislation and sectoral regulators, including the RBI’s FREE-AI framework for finance.A sound governance framework should include clear accountability for each system, regular testing for bias and accuracy, documentation of decisions, and human oversight, especially for credit, employment, or health outcomes. Cybersecurity must also be addressed: in IBM’s 2025 study, only 37% of Indian organisations had AI access controls, nearly 60% lacked AI governance policies or were still developing them, and shadow AI added about ₹1.79 crore to the average breach cost. Transparency with customers and employees about where AI is used strengthens trust.Managing change and bringing people alongTechnology adoption ultimately depends on employees’ willingness to use it. In BCG’s 2025 survey, 92% of Indian employees used AI regularly, the highest of 11 markets, yet 48% feared job displacement within a decade, and only 36% of employees globally felt adequately trained. Dismissing such concerns undermines morale. Leaders should communicate openly about the intended role of AI, emphasise augmentation where that is the objective, and commit to retraining where roles change.Involving frontline staff in design and testing improves both quality and acceptance. Training should be practical and continuous: regular use was markedly higher among employees who received at least five hours of training with coaching. Incentives should reward the use of new tools. Where change management is neglected, even technically excellent systems are quietly ignored.Finally, AI implementation is an ongoing discipline rather than a one-time project. Pilots should have defined success criteria and fixed timelines. Pilots that meet targets should be scaled with investment in integration, monitoring, and maintenance, since models degrade. One study found temporal quality degradation in 91% of the model–dataset combinations it tested. Those that do not should be concluded promptly, with lessons recorded. Tracking return on investment against defined KPIs, which McKinsey associates with bottom-line impact, and reporting it transparently sustains commitment and guides future spending.Fearless legend or grounded realist? headline: India, Nepal sign eight MoUs across space, security, health, and governance during PM Balen Shahs visit
content: New Delhi [India], November 23 (ANI): India and Nepal signed eight Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) spanning space technology, security training, civil service capacity building, health, traditional medicine, sustainable urban development, and agriculture during Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s state visit to New Delhi.The agreements were exchanged following bilateral delegation-level talks between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart at Hyderabad House.In the space and communication sector, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and Nepal’s Ministry of Information and Communication (MOIC) signed an MoU on the Establishment of a Satellite Communication (SATCOM) Network for the Utilization of the South Asia Satellite.Strengthening cooperation in policing and forensic sciences, two agreements were inked: one for Academic and Research Collaboration between the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU) in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, and the Crime Investigation Department of Nepal Police, and another between India's Rashtriya Raksha University (RRU) and the National Police Academy (NPA) of Nepal.To bolster institutional governance, the National Centre for Good Governance (NCGG) under India’s Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances signed an MoU with the Nepal Administrative Staff College under Nepal's Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration for a Capacity Building Training Programme for Civil Servants of Nepal.In the healthcare sector, the two sides signed two pacts: an MoU between India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and Nepal's Ministry of Health and Food Safety on Cooperation in the field of Health and Medicine, alongside a government-to-government agreement on Cooperation in the field of Ayurveda and other Traditional Systems of Medicine.The two governments also signed MoUs on Technical Cooperation in the field of Sustainable Urban Development and on Cooperation in the field of Livestock and Fisheries Development.Earlier in the day, PM Modi recieved his Nepali counterpart at Hyderabad House for the high-level bilateral talks.Highlighting the key engagement between the two leaders, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal wrote in a post on X, "Prime Minister @narendramodi received Prime Minister of Nepal, Rt. Hon’ble Balendra Shah @ShahBalen at the Hyderabad House in New Delhi today.""The two leaders will exchange views on various aspects of India-Nepal relations and explore new avenues to further strengthen and deepen bilateral cooperation," he added.The MEA spokesperson also reflected on previous engagements of the Nepali PM as part of his state visit."State Visit begins on a special note. A ceremonial welcome was accorded to Prime Minister Rt. Hon’ble Balendra Shah @ShahBalen of Nepal at Rashtrapati Bhavan today. It reflected the special warmth and enduring friendship between India and Nepal," Jaiswal wrote in a post on X."A tribute to the timeless legacy of Mahatma! Prime Minister Rt. Hon’ble Balendra Shah @ShahBalen of Nepal offered floral tributes to Mahatma Gandhi at the Raj Ghat Memorial in New Delhi today," another post read.Shah, who arrived in New Delhi on Sunday for a two-day state visit, made his first visit since assuming office in March 2026. (ANI)(This content is sourced from a syndicated feed and is published as received. The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

headline: A Global School operator, GEMS Education collaborates with Swami Vishudhanand Foundation, Varanasi
content: PRNewswireMumbai (Maharashtra) [India], November 23: GEMS Education today announced that the school of Swami Vishudhanand Foundation, Varanasi, has been selected to become a GEMS Education school, following a comprehensive school evaluation and audit process over the last 6 months.The selection recognises what the school already stands for: committed leadership, dedicated teachers, supportive parents and children who are eager to learn. That commitment was seen first-hand when GEMS Director Dr. Ashok Pandey presided over the school's recent Annual Day. The selection is also a statement of belief in what the school can become.Governance, not a franchiseAs a GEMS Education school, the school will come under the governance of GEMS Education as part of the GEMS Millennium Schools brand family. This is not a franchise arrangement, nor one where the GEMS brand is only extended to the school. GEMS Education will be actively involved in the day-to-day governance of the school.GEMS Education will invest in the school to:- elevate teaching and learning in line with GEMS global standards- transform classrooms and learning spaces- build the capability of the school team- upgrade infrastructure to meet the requirements of the future of education- open up multiple curriculum pathways for learners- nurture the overall development of every child.It remains uncompromising on the quality of education and on the safety and well-being of its students and teachers likewise.A Global familyWith this move, the school's learners join the GEMS Education network, home to more than 2 lakh students globally across 176+ nationalities and present in 10 states in India. They gain access to ideas, opportunities and friendships that reach far beyond Varanasi, while the school brings the spirit and heritage of one of India's oldest and most remarkable cities to the network."Today marks the beginning of our new journey in Varanasi. Our aim is simple: that every learner at our institution receives an education that prepares them not just for examinations, but for life and for the world. Teachers are at the heart of every great school, and we look forward to supporting the school's teachers as they grow, lead and inspire. My heartfelt congratulations to the management, the school leadership, the teachers, the parents and, above all, the students. We look forward to writing the next great chapter of this institution together." - Francis Joseph, Group Chief Executive Officer (India), GEMS EducationFor more details, please visit www.gemseducation.com and www.gemseducationindia.com. Email: francis.joseph@gemsedu.in (ADVERTORIAL DISCLAIMER: The above press release has been provided by PRNewswire. ANI will not be responsible in any way for the content of the same.)

headline: Attacks on constitutional institutions erode public trust in democracy: Sonowal
content: Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal on Sunday said questioning the credibility of the Election Commission and other constitutional institutions undermines public confidence in the country's democratic framework.Addressing a citizens' meet organised by civil society groups in Dibrugarh, Sonowal said political differences were natural in a democracy, but parties must not allow narrow political interests to take precedence over the dignity and credibility of constitutional institutions."Every political party has a responsibility to uphold respect and confidence in the country's constitutional and democratic institutions, including the Election Commission (EC)," the Dibrugarh MP said, adding that safeguarding the democratic system was a collective duty.Interacting with prominent citizens from various walks of life, he stressed the importance of an informed and responsible citizenry in strengthening democracy, promoting social development and contributing to nation-building.Sonowal said India's emergence as one of the world's fastest-growing economies reflected its development journey under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership and the vision of 'Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas and Sabka Prayas'.He said politics should primarily be about serving society and ensuring people's welfare rather than pursuing power. He also called for cooperation from all sections of society to accelerate the country's progress."Nation-building is not the responsibility of the government alone; it is a collective responsibility of every citizen. The strength of our democracy lies in the awareness, active participation and sense of duty of its citizens," he said.Referring to Assam's history and identity, Sonowal said protecting the state's language, culture, heritage and the rights of its indigenous communities was a shared responsibility.He also described the issue of illegal foreign nationals as a major concern for Assam, stressing that appropriate action must be taken in accordance with the law and constitutional provisions.(With inputs from PTI).NDA has built trust among people through good governance: Sonowal .Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: AIFF SOM elections: Nine candidates in the fray for four spots on November 23
content: Chennai The elections for Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) at the All India Football Federation (AIFF) will take place on November 23, with nine former players in contention for four spots in the federation’s General Body. In accordance with the National Sports Governance Act, 2025, and the National Sports Governance (National Sports Bodies) Rules, 2026 (together, the “NSG Act and Rules”), the AIFF will have four SOMs – two men and two women – in its General Body, with two members also joining the Executive Committee. Accordingly, a list of 20 men and 20 women was announced earlier this month. It included former India captains Bhaichung Bhutia and I. M. Vijayan among the men, and Oinam Bembem Devi and Ashalata Devi among the women. However, only nine of the 40 shortlisted players ultimately filed their nominations, with Bembem among them. The final list comprises five women and four men. AIFF Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) candidates Men: U. Sharaf Ali, Jo Paul Anchery, Bruno F. Coutinho, Mushtaque Ali Women: Oinam Bembem Devi, Sukla Dutta, Bentla D’Coth, Kalpana Dass, Sradhanjali Samantaray Two candidates, Sradhanjali Samantaray and U. Sharaf Ali, had sought to withdraw their nominations, but their requests were rejected. Sradhanjali, a former India women’s captain, has served as chairperson of both the State Senior and Junior Women’s Selection Committees of the Football Association of Odisha. ALSO READ: AIFF president Kalyan Chaubey calls for ‘mutual accountability’, says former officials should share reports of their tenures https://sportstar.thehindu.com/football/indian-football/aiff-president-kalyan-chaubey-former-officials-share-tenure-reports-praful-patel-new-elections/article71732294.ece Meanwhile, Sharaf Ali was previously the president of the Kerala State Sports Council. He recently came into the spotlight for being among those accused in the sponsorship fraud case involving the proposed visit of football legend Lionel Messi and the Argentina national team to Keralam. “Neither of the above-named candidates appeared personally before the undersigned for submission and authentication of their respective withdrawal requests, and the genuineness of the requests could not be established in accordance with the prescribed procedure,” read a directive issued by Rajeev Sharma, the electoral officer for the polls, explaining the rejection of the two withdrawal requests. Four candidates will be elected to the General Body, of whom two – one man and one woman – will also join the Executive Committee. The AIFF Executive Committee elections are scheduled for December 20. AIFF Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) candidates Men: U. Sharaf Ali, Jo Paul Anchery, Bruno F. Coutinho, Mushtaque Ali Women: Oinam Bembem Devi, Sukla Dutta, Bentla D’Coth, Kalpana Dass, Sradhanjali Samantaray

headline: Srinagar Diary | NC dissent seems to be far from over
content: The dissent in the ruling National Conference in J&K is far from over, and now the disgruntled MLAs are openly questioning the functioning of the Omar Abdullah government. The NC MLA from Pampore Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi recently flagged the governance-related concerns, saying, “It is true that statehood will remove all the obstacles. But there are many things that are not related to statehood and which can be done”. “It was a matter of handling the matters seriously. It was a matter of ending the governance deficit. There is a governance deficit,” he said..JKSSB faces heat over examination cheatingThe Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board (JKSSB) is facing the heat from job aspirants and political parties over the alleged cheating racket detected during the Finance Accounts Assistant (FAA) examination on November 15 in Jammu. On the November 15 exam for 600 Accounts Assistant posts held in J&K, police detected an alleged cheating network involving wireless sets and other electronic communication devices in an exam centre in Jammu. Twenty persons have been detained by police, and a SIT has been constituted by police to investigate the case..Soon, street food hubs in Tangmarg, KathuaThe Omar Abdullah government has approved `9.85 crore for setting up two street food hubs at Tangmarg in Baramulla and Lakhanpur in Kathua. The projects aim to provide hygienic spaces for street vendors while improving public facilities at two important tourism and entry points of the UT. According to the approved proposal, `3.81 crore will be spent on a street food hub at Tangmarg, while `6.04 crore has been earmarked for a street food hub at Lakhanpur, near the state tax office building and the bus stand. The projects will be funded through PM SVANidhi and the Capex Budget.Fayaz waniOur correspondent in Jammu and Kashmirfayazwani123@gmail.com.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: Bija and Bindu: What the Itihasas Teach Us About the Continuity of Governance
content: Author: Dr. Bharat Dash | Upasana TendulkarStorytelling frameworks offer different ways of building a compelling narrative. Pixar emphasises conflict, character and change; the Hero's Journey follows the protagonist through transformation and return. The Natyasastra, India's foundational treatise on dramaturgy, asks a different question altogether: how does a story accommodate change while sustaining continuity? Applied to the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, this question becomes a lens not just on storytelling, but on governance itself - on how legitimate authority survives interruption, exile and crisis without dissolving.Artha-prakrti: The architecture of a storyIn Chapter 21, the Natyasastra describes Artha-prakrti - five elements that carry a dramatic plot towards fulfilment: Bija, Bindu, Pataka, Prakari and Karya. Bija, the seed, is the initial seed from which the principal action grows, holding within it the potential of the entire narrative. Bindu, a drop or point, sustains the continuity of that action when it is temporarily interrupted - the story may turn elsewhere, but its thread is never severed. Pataka and Prakari are subsidiary developments that enrich the narrative, and Karya is the eventual fruit of the action.Of these, Bija and Bindu offer a particularly instructive pair: the seed that sets a crisis in motion, and the continuity that carries legitimate order through it.The Ramayana: A throne that never falls vacantConsider Ayodhya. The Bija here is a succession crisis - Kaikeyi's boons, Dasaratha's anguish, and Rama's exile to the forest for fourteen years. By ordinary logic, a kingdom without its rightful king should drift into disorder. Yet the Ramayana offers one of the most striking governance devices in Indian literature: Bharata, though urged by many to take the throne, refuses to rule in his own name. He places Rama's sandals - the paduka - upon the seat of power and governs as a regent in their service, from Nandigrama, outside the capital itself.This is Bindu in its purest administrative form. The principal action - Rama's rightful kingship - is suspended, but never discarded. Governance continues without interruption precisely because Bharata understands that legitimacy does not reside in the person who happens to occupy the throne, but in the continuity of rightful authority itself. When Rama returns, there is no vacuum to fill and no rupture to repair - only a thread, carefully sustained, now rejoined. It is this continuity, as much as the victory over Ravana, that makes Rama Rajya - not Rama's war, but Rama's rule - the civilisational ideal of Karya, the fruit the entire narrative was building towards.The Mahabharata: Exile without erasureThe Mahabharata offers a parallel. Its Bija is an act of institutional injustice - the rigged dice game that strips Yudhisthira of his kingdom and sends the Pandavas into thirteen years of exile. Here too, the throne is occupied, but legitimacy is not forgotten: the Pandavas spend their exile not in obscurity but in sustained engagement - forging alliances, acquiring knowledge, and preparing for a return to governance rather than retreating from it. Their claim is the Bindu that runs beneath the Udyoga Parva's diplomacy and the Kurukshetra war itself.Woven through this principal action are the Pataka and Prakari - subsidiary episodes that do not advance the plot directly but deepen its meaning. Vidura's counsel to Dhrtarastra, collected as the Vidura Niti, is exactly this kind of subsidiary strand: it does not move the story forward, yet it enriches the narrative with a sustained meditation on statecraft, the duties of a ruler, and the dangers of a king who hears but does not heed wise counsel.The Karya of the Mahabharata, tellingly, is not the war's end but what follows it. On his deathbed, Bhisma delivers the Rajadharma section of the Santi Parva to the newly enthroned Yudhisthira - an extended discourse on the duties, restraints and responsibilities of governance. The epic's true fruit, in other words, is not conquest but counsel: a king instructed in how to rule justly, precisely at the moment he is most capable of forgetting it.Continuity as the architecture of statecraftRead together, both itihasas suggest that governance, like drama, survives disruption not by resisting change but by sustaining an unbroken thread of legitimacy through it. The throne may be vacant, the ruler may be in exile, the kingdom may be shaken - yet governance continues wherever its underlying purpose is honoured rather than merely its outward form.This is a principle with contemporary resonance. Institutions, like kingdoms, inevitably change leadership, strategy and form. What endures is not the specific decisions, but whether each new phase honours the founding purpose it inherited - whether, in the language of the Natyasastra, there remains a Bindu connecting what is new to what came before.Change in continuity. Continuity in change.This may be the deeper lesson the Itihasas offer governance: that institutions, like stories, are not undone by interruption. They are undone only when the thread connecting their present to their founding purpose is allowed to snap. Good governance, like good storytelling, is the art of making sure it never does.This is the spirit in which Bharat Ki Soch works. Its six pillars, Governance among them, rest on the belief that India's inherited wisdom is a living resource, not a relic. Like Bharata's paduka on the throne, the platform keeps the founding purpose present while institutions, policies and ideas evolve around it. Its task is to be the bindu of our times: carrying the seed of Bharatiya thought forward, so that what is new always remembers what it grew from.Dr. Bharat Dash, Professor and Dean Sri Sri University lead guide of Bharat Ki Soch; Upasana Tendulkar, Bharatanatyam dancer and IKS Researcher; Views presented are personal.

headline: Marvels of India - CHOLA ADMINISTRATION
content: The Chola administration was remarkable for combining a strong monarchy with unusually detailed village self-government, documented through contemporary inscriptions. Its institutions managed revenue, justice, irrigation, temples and local committees with written rules and accountability.Decentralised Local GovernanceVillages were not merely administrative units. The Urs (non-Brahman villages), Sabhas (Brahman settlements) and Nagarams (merchant towns) handled local affairs. The state supervised them but allowed substantial local autonomy, making governance participatory and responsive.The Uttaramerur SystemThe Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I, dated 919 and 921 CE, record detailed rules for electing committee members, including eligibility, disqualifications and functions.Committees and AccountabilityElected committees (variyams) managed specific duties such as gardens, tanks, justice and temple affairs. Rules limited tenure, prescribed qualifications and excluded persons with certain misconduct or financial irregularities. These features promoted transparency and prevented concentration of power.Revenue and AdministrationAt the centre, the king was assisted by officials and a structured bureaucracy. Land revenue was carefully assessed and recorded, while local assemblies often collected revenue and maintained irrigation works, linking imperial administration with village-level capacity. Historian K. A. Nilakanta Sastri's study remains a foundational scholarly exploration of these institutions.

headline: Pioneer In Short
content: Ramrao Sakharam Wadkute passes awayRajya Sabha MP Ramrao Sakharam Wadkute, 72, died here early on Sunday following a cardiac arrest. He was admitted to AIIMS Delhi after complaining of chest pain. Hailing from Hingoli district in the Marathwada region of Maharashtra, Wadkute was elected to the Rajya Sabha on a BJP ticket in March this year. President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Vice President and Rajya Sabha Chairman CP Radhakrishnan and BJP President Nitin Nabin condoled the death. “Deeply saddened by the demise of Rajya Sabha MP Shri Ramrao Sakharam Wadkute Ji. He was dedicated to the cause of public welfare and made valuable contributions to the development of Maharashtra and the nation,” the President said on social media.

headline: Alliance Aims For Victory In Kakinada Corporation Elections
content: Kakinada: Rajya Sabha member Sana Satish Babu said victory for the alliance was the goal in the Kakinada Municipal Corporation (KMC) elections and called for coordination among its leaders.He campaigned in Kakinada on Sunday along with Kakinada MP T. Uday Srinivas, Kakinada Rural MLA Pantham Nanaji, MLC Perabathula Rajasekhar and others.Satish Babu said the state was moving forward under Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu’s leadership, with a focus on welfare, development and good governance.He expressed confidence that public trust in the government's administration and development initiatives would translate into support for alliance candidates in the KMC elections.
